Following an election in which voters responded in historic fashion to rising prices — due mostly to Trump’s tariffs and Trump’s war on Iran — President Donald Trump has decided to jack up prices even further by launching a series of newly introduced tariffs. The new tariffs span 14 countries or other trading partners.

It has been revealed that first of all, the big names here are China and the European Union. As if the prices of all kinds of goods haven’t gone up enough, Trump decided to raise the tariffs on Chinese products from about 20% to about 40%. Don’t expect importers and retailers to eat those costs. Those will certainly be passed on to consumers, even if not fully.

Industry observers note that the tariff on products produced in the EU is 15%, which is exactly the maximum tariff agreed to in a 2025 negotiation between the US and the EU. I imagine the EU didn’t anticipate the US turning around and implementing the maximum tariff a year later….

In addition to China and Europe, Trump added tariffs onto products produced in Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam.

According to recent reports, “The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the latest rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations,” The Guardian reports. “Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.”.

Industry observers note that it looks like Trump and team are happy to keep jacking up prices on US consumer goods into 2027, even just after the total blue tsunami that just swept the nation. It seems that Trump just doesn’t care, and is stuck in a 1970s-era ideology around the economy, trade, and tariffs. And we’ll all pay the price for that.

Latest Update: These Are The Non-Car Vehicles You've Crashed

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that crashing a car is a nightmare of physics, emotion and bodily injury.
  • Unsurprisingly, the Honda ATC makes multiple appearances in the comments section.
  • Man, they really don't make them like these vehicles anymore, and thank god.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that crashing a car is a nightmare of physics, emotion and bodily injury. The seriousness of the forces involved rarely make for a funny story. Luckily, these stories are not that. Earlier this week we asked you what vehicles you've crashed that were not cars, and it's clear some of you had childhoods built on survivor bias. Well, I, for one, am glad you survived ditching mountain bikes off of mountains and crashing lawnmowers into houses. Not just because you're still alive but, most importantly, you're alive and contributing to Jalopnik. That's right, you're still here for a very good reason.

Unsurprisingly, the Honda ATC makes multiple appearances in the comments section. Those three-wheeled off-roading vehicles are up their with lawn darts in the damage they caused Gen Xers. They were eventually banned in the U.S. because of the carnage. But you don't need to buy a dangerous vehicle to make it dangerous. Other interesting entries: a gas grill, a horse and a homemade go-kart.

Man, they really don't make them like these vehicles anymore, and thank god.

Just remembered the weirdest thing I've crashed.

My dad had some land in West Virginia. There was a tiny river there and it had some very mild rapids that were more of a ford than a rapids, because it was no more than a foot deep. My sister and I would inflate air mattresses and ride them down the "rapids" normally joined by a dog riding a surfboard that was just a piece of foam shaped like one. Most of the time, the dog made the rapids fine, while my sister and I would run into rocks and the like with the air mattresses. Normally after a week of running the rapids, the air mattresses would be completely ruined by running into branches and sharp rocks.

In a recent development, growing up, dad got a riding lawnmower (Sears 10 hp). Dad morphed it into also being a snow plow with weights on the rear wheels, a homemade plow and a lever to lift and lower it. We had it for years and we took absolutely no care of it other than making sure it had oil before we cranked it up.

According to recent reports, one day, it went missing. By this time, it was at peak jank, with a pull starter, blades that never stopped and an uneven deck that was set to dang near chopping up the roots of the grass. It didn't take Columbo to figure how where it was, as we traced a scalped path through many neighbors' lawns and to the river about 1/2 mile away, where the path of 5 O-clock shadow grass ended and the river began. Some drunk teenager discovered that the brake pedal was disconnected, but didn't discover the way to stop it was to drop it into low gear and turn off the engine.

Sources indicate that oh jeez, that's a list. Dirt bikes of all sizes, same with quads a trike or two, several flavours of boat including a canoe (that shoal jumped in front of me!) but probably the most memorable, or at least the most story worthy is the scooter my buddies dad rented for us when we went on a joint family vacation to Cancun back in the late 90s.

In a recent development, he rented four, two for me and my friend, one for him and one for the older brother and we went ripping around Playa Langosta the way three teens and an adult that branded himself the 'fun' dad could. Getting progressively dumber and riskier as the afternoon wore on. Eventually as the rental time was running out we decided to make a race of it and I was confident enough after a few hours of pinning that little 50cc Honda that I figured I could lean it like a race bike around a corner.

I could not and luckily came away with it with minimal road rash and a major ol bruise on my shoulder.

Industry observers note that the scooter was not so lucky, nor was the magazine stand it slid into. Fortunately insurance had been purchased, unfortunately fun dad was not so fun the remaining days of the trip.

It has been revealed that I've had my share of mountain bike crashes. The most recent bad one was on a slightly downhill rock field (a bunch of bowling ball sized boulders packed into the trail for 60 feet as a technical feature).

I was going a little too fast, got off the proper line, and went down on my side. Normally this wouldn't be a significant deal except rock fields are not very forgiving.

I cracked a couple of ribs which was problematic in that this trail didn't have any short cuts out so I had to ride another 8 miles or so in not very good condition as it was very painful to breathe.

I was sore for a couple months. I also learned to no longer judge NFL QBs who wear flack jackets to protect their ribs. Most painful injury I've ever had. You just have to gut it out.

Back in the '80's my uncle had a farm that I would go work/play on in the summer. My uncle and cousins had just gotten four ATC200 three wheelers that Spring and my cousins and I were all super excited to race 'em all over the farm that summer. I get up there right after school ends and immediately we're off riding through ditches, bombing across fields and having a blast. The big red barn on the farm was at the top of a steep hill with a gravel drive up to and around it. We'd practice to screaming up the gravel drive and as it leveled out, use the negative G-force to whip the tail out into a lurid slide/drift all the way around the barn. On the other side of the barn was the Milking House, so you'd carry the slide between the two buildings with the echo of the screaming 4 stroke bouncing off the walls. Gaining confidence in this technique, we would just continually elevate the speed. First getting air at the top of the hill, then starting the slide later and eventually clipping apexes and throwing gravel everywhere. This abruptly came to an end when I came up the hill the fastest I'd ever gone, got a late start in my slide, went way too wide and clipped the front corner of the milking house on the other side of the barn. The rear axle of the ATC snapped, throwing me over the bars into the side of the milking house and onto the gravel in a heap. This led to the saying in our family, "that boy couldn't hit the broad side of a barn, but sure can nail a milking house!".

It has been revealed that I crashed a Honda ATC when I was maybe 11 or 12 years old. Going way too fast in a large horse pasture when I hit a large dip. Flipped me over, and I'm lucky it didn't land on me. Walked away with a black eye and some scrapes and bruises. 0/10 – do not recommend.

Gen X survivor checking in: if you haven't flipped or nearly paralyzed yourself with a Honda 3-wheeler ATC, you're not really one of us.

From Black Mac and cdoggyd and BuddyS and others (so many others).

My dad built me a homemade go-kart with a 5-hp Briggs & Stratton engine. This was no professional shifter kart chassis. It's exactly what you envision when you think "homemade." Only the right rear wheel was powered. We would take it to the local elementary school on weekends because it had a really large asphalt playground out back and no gates. I'd rip laps for a while until I got tired and we'd go home.

I always went clockwise around the lot. Then one day, I decided I wanted to turn left like my heroes in NASCAR. I got a nice lesson in centrifugal force with the powered wheel now on the inside. It pushed me wide and I hit the curb that separated the asphalt lot with the grass field. I did my best Tony Hawk impression as I did a curb grind for several feet on the floor of the cart. What really stood out to me later is that luckily it happened where it did and not the other side of the lot which would have submarined me under a metal bench face first.

It has been revealed that there isn't anything that moves I probably haven't crashed. Motorcycles, boats, 4 wheelers, snowmobiles, sleds, coaster wagons, bicycles, wheelbarrows, gas grill, and more. Even hit the house with a lawn mower. I learned a zero steer mower sometimes has "zero" steer on wet grass.

Raleigh Chopper. Tore-off a toenail (riding true 1969 style – barefoot in bellbottoms) and broke a tooth. Good times!

Golf carts are my greatest fear in the world because I watched too many camp counselors drive them like demo derby cars. More than once I saw someone try to do a J-turn on one and roll it over and I was certain I just watched someone die.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Mayor of the East Midlands is backing a £47.55 million investment to bring 189 battery-electric buses to the region, replacing older diesel vehicles and helping to improve air quality.

Members of the East Midlands Combined County Authority’s (EMCCA’s) Board have today backed aims to fund fresh buses and charging equipment at depots across Derby, Derbyshire, Nottingham, and Nottinghamshire.

The funding would cover the cost of upcoming vehicles and the charging infrastructure needed to run them, helping operators move away from diesel over the coming years.

Industry observers note that mayor Claire Ward said, “Buses are part of everyday life for thousands of people across our region. They get people to work, help students get to college, and make it easier to see friends and family or get to the shops.

Recent findings suggest that “I want people to have public transport they can rely on, and electric buses mean that fares will not be driven by high fuel prices. They are also cleaner: replacing older diesel buses will cut emissions and improve the air we breathe, while making sure our bus services keep pace with the needs of the people who use them.”.

Industry observers note that “The East Midlands needs to reach net zero by 2050, and changes like this are how we get there. This investment will allow us to make progress while supporting better public transport for people across our region.”.

The four schemes are worth more than £100m in total, with EMCCA contributing £47.55m towards the cost of the buses and charging equipment.

The proposed contributions are:.

Work is expected to take place between 2026 and 2029.

EMCCA is also investing in bus routes, stops and stations, including better lighting and real-time information displays to help passengers plan their journeys.

Recent findings suggest that the Board approved £20.4m towards 44 smaller schemes included in the Bus Corridor Infrastructure and Customer Experience 2026-27 Capital Programme. These include renewal and expansion of real-time passenger information at bus stops and stations, improved lighting, audio-visual display equipment, and other measures to improve passenger comfort, accessibility, and safety.

According to recent reports, board members also approved a £53m fund until March 2029 towards an Integrated Transport Measures and Pinch Points Programme. Eligible activity includes bus shelter refurbishment, bus stop improvements, pedestrian and passenger accessibility measures, passenger information displays, dropped kerbing, traffic signaling, and bus stop enforcement measures.

EMCCA’s transport team will now produce a delivery plan outlining the programme and interventions proposed.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, according to the seller, the 454 V8 was rebuilt and received a replacement camshaft roughly 5,000 miles ago.
  • The Fisher body tag shows that the pickup was originally painted Placer Gold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you're shopping for El Caminos, then this 1971 example should pique your interest. Listed on Bring a Trailer, the pickup has 47,000 miles on the odometer and features a 454 substantial-block V8 paired with a four-speed manual transmission. The El Camino in question has been with the seller since 1992 and comes with the build sheet (albeit a tattered one) and a Nevada title.

According to recent reports, according to the seller, the 454 V8 was rebuilt and received a replacement camshaft roughly 5,000 miles ago. BaT's description notes that the car's true mileage can't be verified, but that hasn't stopped potential buyers from placing their bids, with the highest bid sitting at $8,500 at the time of writing.

The Fisher body tag shows that the pickup was originally painted Placer Gold. The body, as you can see from the pictures, has since been refinished in red, with black striping on the hood. There are chrome details on the bed rails and wheel openings, as well as chrome bumpers and a drop-down tailgate. Locking pins secure a cowl-induction hood, which was added later. Completing the exterior are 14-inch Rally-style wheels fitted with derby-style hubcaps and wrapped in BFGoodrich white-letter tires.

On the inside, the cabin has black vinyl seats with color-matched carpeting, door panels, and dashboard. And per the Fisher body tag (trim code 706), this El Camino appears to have left the factory with a black vinyl interior. Other highlights include power steering and brakes, a Muncie shifter, a center console, and a Pioneer cassette player.

According to recent reports, if you came across this listing earlier, you probably wondered why BaT hadn't listed the car with an SS 454 headline if it was the real deal. There was certainly a lot of activity in the comment section, with doubts surrounding the car's authenticity. Much of the discussion centered on documenting the drivetrain, with commenters coaching the seller on where to find the partial VIN stamped on the engine block.

According to recent reports, the more knowledgeable commenters helped resolve the question after the seller posted photos of the VIN stamp on the block, the rear end, and the Posi tag. User ssterry commented, "Congratulations! Photos #129-131 should be more than adequate to convince BaT that this El Camino was born an SS!" BaT agreed, writing in a November 25 comment, "We've reviewed the additional media, and have updated the listing to reflect that the car is an El Camino SS 454.".

Sources indicate that as you may know, the 454 found its way into a lot of Chevy trucks, including car-based utes like the El Camino. But unlike the more coveted 1970 LS6-equipped models, 1971 SS 454s used the LS5 version of the big-block V8. Even though the LS5 doesn't have the LS6's numbers, the 454 LS5 is still a fairly robust powerplant, rated at 365 gross horsepower and 465 pound-feet of torque (or 285 hp and 390 lb-ft SAE net) for the 1971 model year. Pair that with the four-speed stick, and you have yourself a brilliant excuse for skids and donuts.

According to recent reports, the Nevada-based seller appears to be new to the platform. But the comments and the seller's interaction with them have really helped settle the SS question. Get in the mix and place a bid if you're interested. The auction ends on Saturday, November 28.

Covering TOPCon, XBC, HJT, and Perovskite-Silicon Tandem Technologies; Over 1,000 Automated Module Lines Delivered Globally, More Than 40 in North America.

RE+ 2026 was held at the Las Vegas Convention Center from November 17 to 19. Driven by the U.S. IRA policy that fuels domestic PV capacity expansion amid diversified cell technology roadmaps, SC Solar showcased turnkey automation solutions for high-efficiency modules, including TOPCon multi-cut, BC, HJT, and perovskite-silicon tandem. The team held face-to-face business discussions with global manufacturers on factory planning, equipment configuration, process adaptation, and production line optimization.

Sources indicate that in 2026, the U.S. solar market continued to evolve amid sustained demand and structural adjustments. According to a report released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Wood Mackenzie, the United States added 11.4 GW of solar capacity in the second quarter, up 45% year over year, with utility-scale projects accounting for most of the increase. An SEIA brief updated in September 2026 put U.S. domestic module nameplate manufacturing capacity at approximately 75.3 GW per year. While installation demand remained substantial, the pace of manufacturing capacity expansion moderated. Changes in market competition, policy and investment conditions raised the bar for factory operations and cost control.

For PV manufacturers, capacity expansion requires balancing the need for rapid commissioning with long-term operating value. Key priorities for equipment providers include matching equipment solutions closely to product processes, reducing losses across production-line workflows, improving yield during ramp-up and long-term operation, and lowering manufacturing costs. Drawing on years of project implementation experience in China and overseas, SC Solar combines R&D with the practical needs of factories, providing robust support for PV manufacturing in North America through turnkey automation solutions.

At this year’s exhibition, SC Solar presented customized module automation solutions for the distinct manufacturing needs of TOPCon multi-cut, BC and HJT technology pathways. Integrating production, logistics and digital management, the solutions demonstrated coordinated factory-wide capabilities spanning module manufacturing, warehousing, packaging and truck loading and delivery. Through process adaptation and system integration, they help customers coordinate production planning and factory operations. At the exhibition, the SC Solar team held in-depth discussions with visiting customers and partners on fresh factory planning, upgrades to existing production lines and operational optimization. The team also explored equipment selection and solution configurations for specific project scenarios, laying a solid foundation for future cooperation.

With years of experience in the U.S. market, SC Solar continues to build on its project delivery and customer service expertise. Since 2017, the firm has delivered more than 40 PV module production lines to the U.S. market and established its U.S. subsidiary in 2024. Supported by a local technical service team and spare parts warehouse in Texas, SC Solar provides technical training, operations and maintenance (O&M), capacity upgrades, spare parts supply and remote diagnostics, continually strengthening service support throughout the operating life cycle of customers’ production lines.

In a recent development, from equipment delivery to life-cycle services, SC Solar remains focused on the stable operation and sustainable growth of its customers’ factories. Looking ahead, the company will continue to advance technological innovation and strengthen its local service capabilities. Working with partners around the world, SC Solar will turn manufacturing needs into practical, implementable solutions and support the high-quality development of the global PV manufacturing industry.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the shift places upcoming demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments.
  • Sources indicate that “I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:23 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

Sources indicate that the shift places upcoming demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

Sources indicate that “I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”.

Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:.

Sources indicate that enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The firm’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

It has been revealed that “Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he mentioned during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”.

In a recent development, the demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

“What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:.

Sources indicate that modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing latest AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

It has been revealed that netApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most key thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

It has been revealed that the integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

It has been revealed that “Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole said during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”.

Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

It has been revealed that “AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he said during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:.

Sources indicate that as enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

“Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”.

Sources indicate that automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

Industry observers note that “It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability matter,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Helen Yu and Sandeep Singh:.

  • In a recent development, "Top Gear" has been off the air since the most recent run with hosts Chris Harris, Freddie Flintoff, and Paddy McGuinness fizzled out in 2022.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an old British white guy is back at the helm of the biggest car television program in the world. "Top Gear" will return to filming in 2027 with legendary presenter chef Gordon Ramsay as its newly introduced figurehead. The show has been through some fraught years recently, with dozens of presenters coming and going since the Clarkson/Hammond/May trio were forced to scarper off to Amazon's Grand Tour over a decade ago. Ramsay has been a staple of international television cookery since his Hell's Kitchen and Kitchen Nightmares reveals hit the airwaves in 2004. The three-star Michelin chef has had a part in 24 different television programs, largely focused on the food prep and hospitality industries, while his restaurant group owns some 24 international locations. He's famous, is what I'm saying.

In a recent development, "Top Gear" has been off the air since the most recent run with hosts Chris Harris, Freddie Flintoff, and Paddy McGuinness fizzled out in 2022. My personal favorite era was the 2018-2019 run, with Harris showing off his skills opposite Rory Reid and Matt LeBlanc. There's no word yet as to who will complete the on-screen personality roster with Ramsay, but he'll probably have pretty good chemistry with just about anybody they pick. The sixty-year-old star is getting on a bit in years, but he seems to be able to chop it up and chew the fat with just about anyone. He's been a charismatic and over-the-top TV guy for decades, and knows what makes a show interesting.

While filming begins next year, the show won't hit the airwaves until 2028, so we still have some time until we can see just what this guy has in store for us. Surely, it'll include some international travel, jovial competition, on-track action with The Stig, and stars in reasonably priced cars. Hopefully at least one of Ramsay's co-presenters is too young to receive a pension, eh?

It has been revealed that "Top Gear" has had some pretty awful fits and starts over the last decade plus, as the BBC has tried to fit in some non-standard car show presenters. The worst of which was almost assuredly radio DJ and producer Chris Evans, who helmed the show in 2016 despite having severe motion sickness and knowing next to nothing about cars. Ramsay, to his credit, is a massive car fanatic. He follows F1 religiously, is frequently seen on the grid before races, and recently competed in the celebrity Lego karting race ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Gordon's collection includes millions of quid worth of Ferraris, McLarens, Porsches, Astons, Land Rovers, and more. Apparently he is frequently seen at Brands Hatch driving his BAC Mono track weapon, which certainly endears me to his sensibilities. He has noted that his love of the Ferrari brand was inspired by the TV show Magnum P.I., and he has owned dozens of cars from the brand, including a pair of LaFerrari (coupe and Aperta), an SP2, an SP3, an 812 Superfast, an F12 Tour de France, and more.

Ramsay was a guest on the old Top Gear (when they still had the Cool Wall in the studio) during the first season of the show's original run, airing on December 22 of 2002, back when he was still in his 30s. He had some amusing anecdotes, especially about cooking with car engine. When he took the old Suzuki Liana out around the Dunsfold test track, he looked pretty darn competitive on a dry day. In the end he put down a 1-minute 50-second lap, which tied him with Jeremy Clarkson's best, and just a tick shy of Jay Kay's board leading spot.

Sound off in the comments with your thoughts on Ramsay as presenter, and who you think the BBC should pair with Ramsay for the best results. Are you excited about Top Gear's return? Do you think it'll stick around for a while with Gordon at the helm? I just hope it's good. There hasn't been any good car television lately!

Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna said the program seeks to deepen the organization's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

It has been revealed that the company first debuted a new approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna noted.

"Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," noted Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world.".

Sources indicate that cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the firm for some time, and the company mentioned it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

In a recent development, in that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The organization remarked that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

Eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna noted its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

According to recent reports, "Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” stated Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide important support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”.

#133815. Europe’s Solar Problem Is No Longer Solar

Europe’s Solar Problem Is No Longer Solar

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The rules, grids, and investment framework around it are struggling to keep up.
  • SolarPower Europe’s September mid-year assessment describes a familiar contradiction: solar is contributing more to energy security and affordability, yet weakening policy support, grid constraints, and insufficient flexibility threaten continued growth.
  • Recent findings suggest that in its September newsletter, the association reported that solar became Europe’s largest electricity source in June and estimated that it avoided more than €30 billion in gas imports for power generation over six months of the Middle East conflict.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Europe’s solar fleet is delivering. The rules, grids, and investment framework around it are struggling to keep up.

SolarPower Europe’s September mid-year assessment describes a familiar contradiction: solar is contributing more to energy security and affordability, yet weakening policy support, grid constraints, and insufficient flexibility threaten continued growth.

Recent findings suggest that in its September newsletter, the association reported that solar became Europe’s largest electricity source in June and estimated that it avoided more than €30 billion in gas imports for power generation over six months of the Middle East conflict. At that point, it forecast a slight contraction in EU solar deployment in 2026.

Europe’s ambition to become an electrostate is stuck in a State of Confusion and will remain unconvincing unless its rules and networks catch up. The challenge is no longer simply building solar. It is connecting it, using it, and making participation easier.

Ukraine’s September auctions illustrate the shift.

Preliminary results showed that a 50 MW solar auction attracted three bids totalling 38.99 MW. A separate 100 MW solar-plus-storage auction attracted 26 bids totalling 385.9 MW.

The terms differed: price ceilings were €0.08/kWh for standalone solar and €0.12/kWh for solar-plus-storage. These were bids, not completed projects. The results demonstrate stronger participation in the hybrid auction—not proof that adding batteries is inherently more profitable.

Physical projects show the transition too. A September report described Romania’s 918 MWh battery under construction and a separate 120 MWh system commissioned at Teiuș. Bulgaria’s Devnya solar plant expanded from 5 MWp to 65 MWp, adding 60 MW/165 MWh of storage.

But batteries are only part of the equation. Schneider Electric Research Institute’s October system-cost analysis models 40,500 scenarios combining distributed solar and batteries with central generation and networks.

Under global-average cost assumptions, optimised scenarios put total electricity-system costs about 10% below the benchmark, rising to as much as 40% below under assumed 2030s technology costs. These are modelled outcomes, not forecasts of European household bills.

The lesson from this manufacturer-sponsored research is coordination: electrifying transport, heating, and industry can improve infrastructure utilisation alongside distributed generation.

Denmark is confronting another bottleneck: access to scarce connection capacity.

Denmark’s October connection-prioritisation reform replaces a simple first-come, first-served approach with categories reflecting societal functions, electrification, and other uses. Within categories, projects placing less strain on the grid can receive priority.

Industry observers note that battery treatment matters. Standalone storage falls in category 3, below renewable generation and electrification in category 2. Qualifying co-located batteries can also fall in category 2.

It has been revealed that storage can increase connection requirements or improve an existing connection’s utilisation. Rules should recognise operation, not merely technology labels.

Europe needs transparent queues, credible project-readiness tests and connection arrangements that reward flexibility—not just faster permitting.

It has been revealed that roofs, station canopies, car parks, and noise barriers already occupy space for another purpose. Adding PV can reduce additional land take, although it does not make generation footprint-free.

Belgium’s Solar Tunnel demonstrates the principle. A 2011 announcement records 16,000 modules installed on a covered section of the Paris–Amsterdam railway near Antwerp, designed to generate 3.3 GWh annually for railway infrastructure and trains.

Industry observers note that at Uden in the Netherlands, bifacial PV forms part of an A50 motorway noise barrier. The EU LIFE project’s monitored results recorded 325.5 MWh over 18 months—approximately 220 MWh annually.

It has been revealed that the assessment also reports lower-than-expected generation and higher-than-anticipated capital costs. Multifunctional infrastructure is promising, not automatically cheaper. Engineering, procurement, and maintenance determine whether combined benefits justify the premium.

The strongest projects preserve their original function while adding electricity: shade plus charging, noise protection plus generation, or water infrastructure plus power. They complement conventional rooftop and ground-mounted solar rather than replace them.

At the other end of the scale, plug-in solar challenges the assumption that participation requires an owned roof and a substantial installation budget.

Germany’s Federal Network Agency provides a simplified administrative route for qualifying systems, with module capacity up to 2,000 Wp and inverter output up to 800 VA.

According to recent reports, registration remains mandatory. Separate network-operator notification is waived under specified conditions, including the unpaid-export arrangement. These administrative thresholds do not override technical or installation-safety requirements.

Germany’s environment agency explains that qualifying devices within technical limits can be commissioned by non-specialists.

That matters because administrative and installation costs can be disproportionate for small systems. Balcony solar offers a route for people without access to a conventional rooftop installation, including some apartment residents.

In a recent development, it does not replace large-scale generation or remove mounting, electrical-safety, building-consent, and country-specific requirements. Its importance is accessibility: proportionate regulation makes small-scale participation possible.

Europe needs large projects, distributed generation, solar-equipped infrastructure, accessible household systems, batteries, and flexible demand.

Writing from Down Under, the parallel is clear. High rooftop-solar penetration is reshaping Australian daytime demand and electricity prices. The response is batteries, flexible demand, and market rules that reward them.

Industry observers note that the choice is not between ambition and practicality. Practical rules are how ambition becomes deployment.

Prof Ray Wills is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.

Tesla's Safety Lawsuits Never Reach Courts Because Of The Fine Print At Purchase

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While Tesla faces legal challenges from a who's who of governmental oversight bodies, Tesla has been able to repeatedly dodge private citizens complaints through a seemingly ironclad arbitration clause found in all latest Tesla sales contracts.
  • In a recent development, in fact, civil lawsuits regarding deadly and damaging crashes seem to end in quiet settlement after quiet settlement.
  • Sources indicate that the pivotal line item can be found in customer contracts regarding forced arbitration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Tesla faces legal challenges from a who's who of governmental oversight bodies, Tesla has been able to repeatedly dodge private citizens complaints through a seemingly ironclad arbitration clause found in all latest Tesla sales contracts.

In a recent development, in fact, civil lawsuits regarding deadly and damaging crashes seem to end in quiet settlement after quiet settlement. When they don't, the payout is massive, like the $243 million judgement after a 2019 Autopilot crash in Florida. So what is Tesla hiding behind closed doors?

Sources indicate that the pivotal line item can be found in customer contracts regarding forced arbitration. As the San Francisco Chronicle points out in its investigation, Tesla quietly settled 920 consumer cases in the last 10 years; "twice as many as the nine other top 10 U.S. automakers combined." So far, in the public court records and case logs the Chronicle collected, it found Tesla managed to skirt 12 attempted class action lawsuits because of its ironclad arbitration clause.

Recent findings suggest that the specific arbitration agreement under each of those sections claims that if an matter isn't resolved within 60 days of occurrence, the owner agrees to have any issue resolved via arbitration. Owners are unable to bring about any class-action lawsuits against the firm.

Two attorneys found that out when they were hired to take on Tesla. The initial class-action lawsuit they brought against Tesla had 12 individuals behind it which ,due to the agreement, forced it to be broken down into 12 separate arbitrations. And as is the way in arbitration, Tesla wasn't required to supply discovery evidence, especially if it considered any data "proprietary information," so the problem disappeared without any admittance of wrongdoing.

The approach works so well for Tesla that other automakers are beginning to take notice and add similar agreements to their own vehicles or taking cases into arbitration as well. Rivian, also an electric vehicle maker, has already done so.

Sources indicate that owners can at least opt out within 30 days of signing the agreement by sending a letter to a Tesla P.O. Box in Fremont, California. How many of them knew that was a possibility is likely low, as even the Chronicle found most Tesla owners had no idea it was there. To truly see the entire picture you should read the entire investigation by the Chronicle, and watch its accompanying video.

It has been revealed that it's a stark reminder of how key it is to read the terms of service to everything you purchase and use before signing. Otherwise, you end up in a losing battle against Tesla, or Stan's unfortunate situation.

HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment aims against the manufacturer’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information manufacturer, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

Industry observers note that clinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from articles sourced from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the company claims the solution integrates with all EHR providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

In a recent development, clinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson noted the company's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

The company has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

In a recent development, three months ago, the firm rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations, the company mentioned. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

In a move to develop context-aware AI, the manufacturer acquired Wellsheet in June. The health technology company aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside.

Recent findings suggest that “The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

According to recent reports, “Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she said.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”.

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

San Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, New Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

Recent findings suggest that hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, he remarked. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak remarked.

"We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak mentioned.

He added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and highlights exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians.".

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

ClinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he stated, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by swiftly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to quickly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he said.

The AI solution can quickly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak said.

One patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak noted. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

"We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he said.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

Industry observers note that generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and providing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act swiftly, Hallak stated.

Industry observers note that "From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he remarked.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

Recent findings suggest that "It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals said it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

It has been revealed that going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also plans to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

Industry observers note that "These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak noted.

Recent findings suggest that the medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he said.

Sources indicate that elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott said.

Industry observers note that "Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, mentioned. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, audi Sport has put out an incredible amount of renowned performance cars over the years, but without a doubt the most beloved by enthusiasts are the various RS Avants. From the original RS2 to the RS4 and RS6, the Avant wagons have far outweighed sedans when it comes to production volume and cultural impact, even if you count the recent four-door RS5s. Some generations of RS4 and RS6 never even received sedan variants, and the last RS6 sedan (the V10-powered C6) went out of production in 2010. That role was filled by the RS7 four-door coupe, and there's no more A7 anymore, either.

For the upcoming RS6 version of the current C9-gen A6, which has been running around testing in camouflage for quite a long time now, Audi is bringing back the RS6 sedan in addition to the Avant. Our spies took a newly introduced batch of shots of the RS6 sedan looking even closer to production while testing at the Nürburgring, looking particularly bodacious with its widebody clearly visible despite the camo wrap. To assuage the worries I know are swirling around in your brains, Audi already confirmed the new RS6 Avant will come to America, so the sedan will just be another flavor to choose from if, for some reason, you're someone who hates wagons like those people who say they have an anti-cilantro gene.

This RS6 sedan prototype doesn't have any fake body panels or other earlier-stage camouflage coverings, with the only thing obfuscating the design being the swirly wrap. The new RS5 is wider than a regular A5 by over 1.5 inches, and the same looks to be true for the RS6. Like the RS5, its larger sibling also has a functional vent in the front fenders ahead of the door, and the flared arches are filled with big wheels that look to be 22s.

Industry observers note that it's got a similar double-diamond pattern to the wide front grille, and the side intakes in the RS6's front bumper look even bigger than the RS5's. Camo is covering the headlights, which will get RS-specific running light designs and animations. There's a cute little lip spoiler on the trunk, and the rear diffuser has two gigantic oval exhaust tips. The taillights should also have RS designs.

In a recent development, the yellow sticker on the rear window confirms that the RS6 will be a plug-in hybrid, and while early rumors and prototypes pointed to the RS6 using the same twin-turbo V6 as the RS5, we know it will use an updated version of the Porsche-derived V8 that's in the current gas-only RS6 (and that's used in PHEV Porsches and Bentleys). With a large battery pack and an electric motor added on, the new RS6 should have at least 700 horsepower and a usable EV range of a few dozen miles. We'll find out for sure when the RS6 debuts at some point in 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tech giant releases a competitive bidding process for up to 150 megawatts of latest Michigan solar energy.

DTE Energy has confirmed looks to add up to 150 megawatts of latest solar energy in Michigan, creating construction jobs, supporting local communities, and saving customers money on fuel costs.

Because solar generation does not require fuel, the new projects will help reduce the company’s exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. The projects will also support DTE’s work to provide customers with energy that is reliable, increasingly clean, and affordable.

According to recent reports, “These projects are an investment in Michigan and the communities we’re proud to serve. By producing more Michigan-made energy that doesn’t require us to purchase fuel, we can help lower energy costs for our customers and reduce our reliance on fuel from outside our state. At the same time, these projects will create good jobs and bring latest investment and tax revenue into local communities, providing more resources for schools, first responders and the services Michigan families count on every day.”.

Recent findings suggest that DTE is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan-based solar generation. The procurement supports the requirements of the settlement agreement in Michigan Public Service Commission Case No. U-21662, approved May 15, 2025.

It has been revealed that projects must achieve commercial operation by June 30, 2030, be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE’s distribution system. Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate. Proposals are due Jan. 19, 2027, and DTE expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

DTE is Michigan’s leading producer of and investor in renewable energy, generating enough clean energy from wind and solar to power nearly 1 million homes. As the manufacturer works toward net zero carbon emissions, it remains committed to growing its renewable energy portfolio while maintaining a balanced mix of energy resources that supports reliability and affordability for customers. DTE’s 2026 Integrated Resource Strategy builds on that commitment, calling for an additional 15 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2042.

Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a new survey highlights.
  • The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) said they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.
  • The survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% remarked they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a new survey highlights.

The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) said they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.

The survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% remarked they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill. And only a quarter (27%) said they completely understand their own health coverage.

That noted, most (79%) of those surveyed said they believe AI can help to improve the healthcare experience overall.

Ratnakar Lavu, chief digital information officer at Elevance Health, told Fierce in an email that because the tech has the ability to promptly surface and parse key data about a member or health need, it can serve as a central piece of the puzzle in making a more personalized experience.

"AI-enabled tools give us the ability to create a unique member context," he said. "Because of this digital technology, we can now truly 'know the person' and proactively work with them to help them manage their healthcare needs.".

For example, 82% of those surveyed said they would like to receive answers about healthcare as swiftly as they can use an app to order a food delivery, and 83% would like to easily access recommendations that pull from their health coverage, individual health needs and financial situation.

Seventy-two percent said they would trust AI for accuracy on at least one type of information, such as an explanation of benefits, cost estimates or details on medication.

However, while many Americans believe AI can play a leading role in driving a better health experience, just 20% noted they right now use the tech regularly as a source of information. And while 72% said they trusted the tech to surface key health information, 33% said they would trust an AI platform to translate their insurance benefits, and 30% said they trust the tech to estimate care costs.

Just 13% said they would trust AI to make diagnoses.

Lavu said that healthcare organizations looking to roll out newly introduced tools need to avoid simply embedding AI into programs for the sake of it, and be transparent about both the use case as well as the role of the human in the loop.

The study also found that women were less likely than men to trust AI, and younger generations were more likely to use it as a source of healthcare information than older groups.

"We have to implement AI at the speed of trust, which means being thoughtful about where AI adds value, not just delivering technology for technology’s sake," he said. "Trust is also earned when AI-enabled programs truly make things easier for the consumer. ".

In a recent development, for example, Elevance Health has deployed an AI-powered program to support utilization management reviews and help drive faster approvals where possible, though AI is not used to make claims denials. It is also leaning on AI for more proactive member engagement initiatives through its digital channels, identifying individuals that would benefit from extra support or who may face gaps in care.

Recent findings suggest that "We start by listening to members and identifying where healthcare is creating the most confusion or friction," Lavu mentioned. "From there, we determine the right solution, which may or may not involve AI. When AI is the right tool, it should fit naturally into familiar interactions and make it easier for members to get an answer or take the next step.".

#133805. MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
