MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • It has been revealed that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • Industry observers note that the findings raise vital questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But fresh research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

It has been revealed that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

Industry observers note that the findings raise vital questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

According to recent reports, "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," claims Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

Sources indicate that the study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

Deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

In 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an important role in carrying away waste products.

According to recent reports, that earlier discovery led to a fresh question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

Industry observers note that previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially notable.

To investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

It has been revealed that each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

Industry observers note that the researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings indicated that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

It has been revealed that the researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

When a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

To measure this response, the researchers showed volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

It has been revealed that in many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Recent findings suggest that once again, the older group demonstrated a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Recent findings suggest that using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes indicates. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have crucial implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

According to recent reports, earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

None of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants showed signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

It has been revealed that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

In a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

While older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

"It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis says. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

Latest Update: At $17,000, Would You Say The Price Is Right For This 1973 V8 Chevy Vega?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to its ad, today's Nice Price or No Dice Vega was once a door prize on the TV game show, "The Price Is Right." Today, it appears nicely restored and has a surprise SBC under its hood.
  • In a recent development, A common way to describe avoidance of an object or idea is the phrase "I wouldn't touch it with a 10-foot pole." The origin of this idiom remains unknown, but a similar, earlier phrase, "not to be handled with a pair of tongs," carries the same meaning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to its ad, today's Nice Price or No Dice Vega was once a door prize on the TV game show, "The Price Is Right." Today, it appears nicely restored and has a surprise SBC under its hood. Let's see if any of you are game to pay its asking price.

In a recent development, A common way to describe avoidance of an object or idea is the phrase "I wouldn't touch it with a 10-foot pole." The origin of this idiom remains unknown, but a similar, earlier phrase, "not to be handled with a pair of tongs," carries the same meaning. In 18th-century Great Britain, 10-foot was frequently substituted with "barge," as barge poles were typically long and thus offered reasonably remote poking opportunities.

I bring this all up because, based on the comments, the 2017 Alfa Romeo Giulia we looked at on Wednesday was a car that some of you wouldn't touch with a 10-foot pole. That was because the car—and Alfa Romeo in general—carries a reputation for frustratingly frequent breakdowns and bank-account-bruising repairs. That being noted, our Giulia's great looks, seemingly good condition, and $7,999 asking price proved a winning combination in the end. That's shown by the 70% 'Nice Price' win it received in the vote.

While not as good-looking as yesterday's Alfa, the 1973 Chevy Vega notchback that stands before us today is an arguably handsome, well-balanced design. The car's mini-Camaro nose and pleasing profile were the best things about it when it released in 1970. Pretty much everything else about the car, however, was snake-bit from the start.

Chevrolet introduced the Vega in late summer 1970 as the brand's upcoming compact car, nominally replacing the Corvair, which had ended its production run a year earlier. Like the Corvair, the Vega was a clean-sheet design, sharing little carryover parts from other GM cars. Also like the Corvair, the Vega proved problematic for the brand.

Sources indicate that the complications that plagued the early model years weren't limited to engineering or production mistakes; even the car's innovative transportation method—shipping it vertically on specially designed train cars—caused unforeseen fluid leaks before the Vegas even reached a dealer. Premature corrosion was another Vega bugaboo, especially in rustbelt states. The biggest problem, though, was with the Vega's SOHC 2.3-liter four-cylinder engine. Built with an alloy block and cast iron head, the engine had no cylinder liners or special wear-resistant coating to keep the bores intact. Chevrolet had to concern recalls on almost every Vega produced to address safety and drivability issues after only two years of production.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, someone has addressed at least the engine issues with this Vega by sending its original motor to the recycler and replacing it with a 350 cubic inch small-block Chevy V8. Could there be a more reliable engine than the tried-and-true SBC?

According to recent reports, that engine looks right at home in the Vega's engine bay and sits unencumbered by unnecessary ancillaries like a power steering pump or an air conditioning compressor. It does have a heater hookup and a larger-than-stock radiator to cool the plus-size engine. Other engine bay items of note include an MDS distributor and coil and a custom brazed-together air intake that flops the filter over one rocker cover.

In a recent development, based on the underneath pictures, the V8 feeds what looks to be the Vega's Opel-sourced four-speed manual gearbox and punky factory rear end, so don't expect dramatics at the drag strip out of this car. According to the ad, the car has around 90,000 miles on the clock, but only a couple thousand of those were added after the engine swap. The seller claims it " Drives great and turns heads.".

A new engine isn't the only update this Vega has seen. At the same time as the heart transplant, this car also got new candy-apple red paint and fresh vinyl seat upholstery. The remaining original parts of the interior—door cards, dash, and carpets—all look to be in suitably good shape. Two cracks, oddly at exactly 12 and 6, mar the factory two-spoke steering wheel, but shouldn't affect its use or safety. The only other potential misstep is a modern stereo head unit that spoils the overall old-school aesthetic.

It has been revealed that on the exterior, all the chrome shines nicely, and the paint appears to be a professionally applied respray. A set of Minilite-esque alloys underpins, and they appear to have reasonably new rubber. As is typical of Facebook Marketplace ads, the ad doesn't mention the car's title status, but given how old of a car it is, we might be able to overlook that.

It has been revealed that as noted, the ad claims this Vega had a run-in with Bob Barker on the daytime TV game show "The Price Is Right." Amazingly, that show gave away a ton of Vegas, though a quick search of the videos I could find from the era didn't turn up any featuring this particular car. We'll just have to imagine that experience, along with the opportunity to win a Tappan range or an all-inclusive seven-day adventure to Bali.

Once we're done with all that, we'll have to come back to reality and decide whether this V8 Vega is worth its $17,000 asking price. Yes, no one would have guessed that on The Price Is Right, but that's what makes this an even more exciting opportunity.

What do you think? Is this refreshed, re-engined Vega worth $17,000 as-is? Or for that price, would you refuse to "come on down!".

Facebook Marketplace out of Astoria, Oregon, or go here if the ad disappears.

Sources indicate that UPDATED: Nov 20 at 1:30 p.m. ET.

The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on new broker enrollments, court documents show.

According to recent reports, according to a filing submitted Thursday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Service will published a withdrawal on the Federal Register. The move follows a court ruling earlier this month in favor of two leading organizations representing brokers, which granted a preliminary injunction on the moratorium.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

Per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

UPDATED: Nov. 5 at 4:30 p.m. ET.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on fresh broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act.".

The court also stated that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

Industry observers note that NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

It has been revealed that "Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," mentioned NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters.".

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," said Walker.

According to recent reports, NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

PUBLISHED: Oct. 15 at 5:15 p.m. ET.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

According to recent reports, CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency said latest brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP says that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment.".

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP mentioned.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization remarked.

NABIP President Mychal Walker stated that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker said in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them.".

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA looks without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

#133800. Tech Report: Hybrids Are a Waypoint, Not the Destination

Tech Report: Hybrids Are a Waypoint, Not the Destination

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An earlier version of this article appeared in The Driven on 15 October 2026.
  • According to recent reports, in January 2024, Toyota chairman Akio Toyoda stated battery EVs would reach at most 30% market share, with the remainder going to hybrids, hydrogen, and combustion vehicles.
  • PHEVs are conditional transition vehicles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An earlier version of this article appeared in The Driven on 15 October 2026. This version has been revised and updated with the most recent registration data.

By Ray Wills, Raphael Wellmann, and Peter Newman.

According to recent reports, in January 2024, Toyota chairman Akio Toyoda stated battery EVs would reach at most 30% market share, with the remainder going to hybrids, hydrogen, and combustion vehicles. Norway’s BEV share was already at about 89% that year. Norway alone cannot settle a prediction about the global market, but it highlights that 30% is no inherent ceiling on BEV adoption.

PHEVs are conditional transition vehicles. They earn their environmental case through verified electric kilometres, not through the presence of a charging port.

Mature markets tell the more revealing story. Once battery-electric vehicles offer sufficient choice, charging confidence, and competitive economics, hybrids do not settle into a permanent share of the market. Hybrids may lead early, peak, and then retreat.

Sources indicate that norway. The year is 2015. Hybrid vehicles had gained material market share and plug-in hybrids were beginning to arrive in volume. In 2017, PHEVs accounted for about 18% of newly introduced registrations. BEV growth temporarily paused, while hybrids benefited from familiar factories, familiar supply chains, and familiar consumer expectation.

Sources indicate that after another PHEV surge in 2020 and 2021, the direction changed. By October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 98.8% of Norway’s new passenger-car registrations. Petrol plug-in hybrids represented just 0.2%, and petrol full hybrids 0.3%. Across the first ten months of the year, BEVs held 98% of the market. Hybrids had not become a permanent destination: they had become marginal in new-car sales.

It would be easy to dismiss Norway as a special case: a small, affluent, and subsidy-supported market.

Sources indicate that singapore has a distinctive vehicle-ownership system, built around Certificates of Entitlement, high ownership costs, and tightly managed taxation. Yet its market also indicates hybrids losing ground as BEVs expand. Conventional hybrids accounted for 28.3% of new registrations in October 2026, while BEVs held 59.6% and PHEVs 6.2%. The monthly figures fluctuate: hybrid share was higher than in August. The longer-term question is whether hybrids retain their earlier prominence as BEVs become mainstream—not whether their share falls every month.

In a recent development, denmark provides another example. In October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 88.2% of all newly introduced passenger-car registrations and 97.4% of households’ new cars. The distinction matters: household purchases and the overall market do not electrify at precisely the same pace. But both now show BEVs becoming the dominant choice.

These three markets are not identical, and their policies are not interchangeable. But they show a repeating shape. In leading electrification markets, hybrid share has not settled into a stable plateau. It has risen, peaked and then declined.

That is what a waypoint looks like.

Sources indicate that for years, Norway was treated as the exception: small, rich, subsidy-heavy, and unrepresentative. But its basic market pattern is now appearing wherever electrification has advanced far enough.

Once the pattern is visible in several unrelated countries, the question becomes whether it is appearing more widely, including in markets still early in the transition.

Trailing-twelve-month registration data across the selected markets show not a world divided between “BEV countries” and “hybrid countries,” but markets at different stages of electrification and following different routes.

Some move relatively directly from combustion vehicles to BEVs. Others pass through a stronger hybrid phase, then a PHEV phase, before BEVs become dominant. In China, PHEVs and range-extended EVs have gained strength alongside BEVs, supported by rapid product cycles, intense domestic competition, expanding charging networks, regulatory settings, and strong domestic manufacturers.

This is not a claim that hybrids have already peaked everywhere. Across the European Union, BEVs accounted for 23.4% of upcoming-car registrations in the first ten months of 2026, while hybrids remained a major part of the market. In Australia, the hybrid share is still close to its high, but in October 2026, BEVs overtook hybrids on a trailing-twelve-month basis for the first time (18.5% vs. 17.6%). The transition remains uneven across countries, buyer types, and vehicle segments.

It has been revealed that the route differs. The starting point differs. The pace differs. The picture that comes out isn’t “some countries like BEVs, others like hybrids.” As BEVs meet more buyers’ needs at competitive cost, hybrids face increasing pressure on their share of fresh-car sales. Whether their absolute sales also fall depends on the size and growth of the market.

There is a practical implication for buyers. A hybrid purchased today in a market that has not yet reached its tipping point may face greater residual-value risk when it arrives on the used market. If new-car demand shifts rapidly towards BEVs while used supply reflects today’s hybrid-heavy sales, resale values may come under pressure.

Fuel prices, tax settings, used-BEV supply, charging access, and export markets will impact, but it is a risk buyers, fleets, and financiers should acknowledge.

If the pattern is visible in the data, why does public discussion so often present hybrids as a permanent pillar of the future vehicle market?

Recent findings suggest that one reason is that the transition is uneven—the future is here, it’s just not well distributed yet. In many countries, people have only seen the rising half of the hybrid curve. The peak and decline have not yet arrived. It is easy to mistake “still growing” for “here to stay.”.

Recent findings suggest that another is that manufacturers with decades of investment in combustion and hybrid platforms have commercial reasons to extend the life of those systems. That behaviour seems rational. Hybrid platforms preserve familiar engines, suppliers, dealer servicing, and factory investments.

But that commercial logic is not evidence that hybrid demand will remain durable once BEVs can do the same job more effectively. As with everything, the biggest cost may come not in going too fast, but in going too slow.

It is also important not to overstate the case against PHEVs. A PHEV that is routinely plugged in can cover much of its owner’s daily driving on electricity. The problem is that many of those PHEVs are not used that way.

Sources indicate that european Commission data from 320,000 PHEVs first registered in 2021 found real-world CO₂ emissions averaging 3.5 times their official type-approval values. The Commission concluded that these vehicles were not being charged and driven electrically as frequently as assumed in laboratory testing.

Firm vehicles are a particular problem. Petrol may be employer-paid, immediate, and simple to use, while home charging is paid by the employee, workplace charging is unavailable, and reimbursement is cumbersome. Under those conditions, the petrol engine becomes the default.

A PHEV is a bridge—but only if people use it to cross from the petrol side to the electricity side.

Sources indicate that the registration data do not say that every hybrid buyer has made the wrong decision. Some households and fleets still need a transitional option. Some regional, towing, remote-area, and high-kilometre uses remain difficult for today’s BEV models and charging networks.

But those are specific use cases that are not representative of the mass market and thus not a reason to preserve combustion systems for everyone.

Conventional hybrids reduce petrol consumption, particularly in stop-start urban driving, but every kilometre still depends on fuel. PHEVs can replace a substantial share of petrol with electricity, but only if they are regularly charged, have enough real-world electric range, and do not unnecessarily run their engine.

BEVs eliminate routine petrol use and are the most energy-efficient option for the expanding share of households and fleets whose driving and charging conditions suit them.

The role of policy is not to pretend that all drivers are identical. It is to make electric driving easier: reliable charging at homes, apartments, workplaces, and regional routes; electricity reimbursement as straightforward as fuel reimbursement; and real-world reporting of petrol use and electric kilometres in PHEV fleets.

It has been revealed that the market is not likely to move from combustion to BEV in exactly the same way everywhere. But as battery-electric vehicles become cheaper, more capable, and easier to charge, the addressable market for hybrids contracts.

Hybrids can help drivers transition from the combustion era into the battery electric era.

But that is all they are, a waypoint towards an electric future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:19 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Sources indicate that cloudera Inc. today confirmed a digital sovereignty package that it noted enables organizations to maintain control over their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure regardless of where workloads run.

Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty combines the tech giant’s Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral SAS, with whom Cloudera recently partnered. The integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments that have no connection to external networks.

Digital sovereignty is becoming a more pressing matter as enterprises move beyond managing data residency to ensuring that the AI models and infrastructure they depend upon remain under their control. McKinsey & Co. reported last year that 71% of the executives it surveyed called sovereign AI an “existential concern” or “strategic imperative.” Cloudera said its own research found that regulation, privacy and data sovereignty requirements rank among the top three barriers to scaling AI.

“As AI becomes more autonomous and embedded in critical operations, enterprises need to know that their data, models, and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change,” Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago remarked in a statement.

It has been revealed that the offering provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments. Those capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union’s AI Act, Digital Operational Resilience Act and Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations.

Governance policies also extend to the enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use in performing tasks. Mistral’s open-weight models can run alongside governed data, enabling organizations to customize models locally and execute agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information.

Cloudera’s modular hybrid cloud architecture enables owners to shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data. Organizations can also selectively apply sovereignty controls to sensitive workloads without imposing the same restrictions across their entire computing estate.

Moor Insights & Strategy Inc. Chief Analyst Patrick Moorhead said AI has raised the bar on data protection. “A manufacturer can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on,” he said in a statement.

Sources indicate that cloudera mentioned it will supplement its Mistral partnership with an ecosystem of sovereign cloud providers and implementation partners. The organization is initially targeting Europe but intends to expand the partner network into other regions and regulatory jurisdictions.

An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an vital difference between human and chimpanzee brain development.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population.
  • Although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an vital difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.

Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer new clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.

Although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.

Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, indicates the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.

Recent findings suggest that "The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is important to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," indicates Johan Jakobsson.

How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene.

According to recent reports, at the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.

It has been revealed that the difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.

Over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.

Methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.

Jakobsson states understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide notable insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference.

According to recent reports, to investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.

Recent findings suggest that when the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 demonstrated strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.

"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," states Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.

Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.

The result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.

"This reveals that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," states Patricia Gerdes.

Latest Clues to Human Brain Evolution.

The team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.

Sources indicate that disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.

The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to vital stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.

Sources indicate that more broadly, the discovery highlights an important principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.

The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.

Researchers now strategy to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.

Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Millions of renters, apartment residents, and condo owners can’t put solar on a roof they don’t control.
  • It has been revealed that rooftop solar assumes you own a roof, can afford a large upfront cost, and can wait through permits and installation.
  • Industry observers note that UL 3700, the Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In Photovoltaic Equipment and Systems, was published in December 2025, and UL Solutions began certifying products to it in January 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Millions of renters, apartment residents, and condo owners can’t put solar on a roof they don’t control. Plug-in solar, also called balcony solar or plug-in PV, offers a workaround: one or more panels connected through a microinverter to an ordinary wall outlet, with no roof work and, in a growing number of states, no utility interconnection application — though, this is only applicable in select states (users should refer to their state laws before installation). A newly introduced safety standard, UL 3700, is helping this market mature, and it comes with a lesson every buyer should learn: a compliant component is not the same thing as a certified system.

It has been revealed that rooftop solar assumes you own a roof, can afford a large upfront cost, and can wait through permits and installation. Plug-in solar flips that. States are responding. As of mid-October, ten states had enacted plug-in solar laws: Utah, Maine, Virginia, Colorado, Maryland, Fresh Hampshire, Connecticut, Vermont, New Jersey, and California. Effective dates vary, with several laws not taking effect until 2027, and New York’s SUNNY Act is awaiting the governor’s signature. Several of these laws require kits to meet a recognized safety standard, and some name UL 3700.

Industry observers note that UL 3700, the Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In Photovoltaic Equipment and Systems, was published in December 2025, and UL Solutions began certifying products to it in January 2026. It exists because rooftop solar standards weren’t written for equipment that homeowners plug in themselves. The safety problems are specific:.

Hoymiles says the HiFlow Pro was built around these challenges and shuts down in 135 milliseconds if it’s unplugged or the grid fails. For comparison, Maine’s law requires shutoff within 0.2 seconds.

Industry observers note that here is the part that matters most for buyers. UL 3700 evaluates a complete system: the microinverter, how it connects, relevant accessories, and the overall configuration, not the microinverter alone. That means compliance for one part doesn’t automatically establish that the whole kit has been certified.

According to recent reports, the HiFlow Pro reveals how this works in practice. Hoymiles describes the microinverter itself as UL 3700-compliant, and it has been widely reported as the first plug-in microinverter in the US to reach that point after its July 15, 2026 launch. The complete HiFlow Pro system has not yet finished certification. Hoymiles says it is pursuing it and expects the process to wrap up in December 2026.

The HiFlow Pro is a plug-in microinverter, so the panels are bought separately or as part of a kit. Per Hoymiles, up to four units can run on separate outlets for up to 1,200 watts, depending on state and local rules, and models range from 360 W to 500 W to fit different legal limits. The manufacturer lists a peak efficiency of 95.5%, a NEMA Type 6 enclosure, an operating range of -40°F to 149°F, a 12-year standard warranty, and monitoring through the S-Miles Home app. It also cites 250,000 hours of reliability testing, and says TIME named the product one of its Best Inventions of 2026.

According to recent reports, follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Plug the unit directly into a wall outlet, not a power strip or extension cord, and use a GFCI outlet if you’re running a larger system on one circuit.

Hoymiles estimates up to 721 kWh a year from a single 360 W unit, modeled at 5.6 peak sun hours a day and about 2,403 kWh from a four-unit system. At 38 cents per kWh, a rate found only in the highest-cost regions, the manufacturer estimates savings of up to about $247 per unit per year and a payback of roughly two years. By our math, that figure assumes about 90% of the power gets used inside the home. Actual savings depend on how much electricity you use during daylight hours, and surplus power may flow to the grid without credit unless your utility offers net metering.

Recent findings suggest that for context, EnergySage puts typical savings from a plug-in kit at $13 to $20 a month at the national average rate of about 18 cents per kWh, and $40 to $50 a month in high-rate states like California, Latest York, and Hawaii. Two limits are worth knowing: the system reduces your bill but doesn’t replace the grid, and it won’t provide backup power in an outage. The federal homeowner solar tax credit also ended on December 31, 2025, so payback estimates shouldn’t assume one.

Rules vary by state, and sometimes by utility. Hawaii, with some of the country’s highest electricity prices, isn’t among the ten states with a plug-in solar law, so renters and condo owners here should check with Hawaiian Electric and their association before buying. Even in states with laws, utilities may ask for notice, and landlord and HOA protections differ.

Prices and product configurations vary by retailer, so check the current listing.

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA plan Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth remarked in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

In a recent development, the star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage prepares and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

It has been revealed that "The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

According to recent reports, UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The firm sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the tech giant stated that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

Industry observers note that "Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the organization said.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company remarked.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the intends available to them," Elevance said.

According to recent reports, "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the manufacturer continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing intends.".

Industry observers note that UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

It has been revealed that the court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer said that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the tech giant's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in aims with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

Recent findings suggest that in a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the organization argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

According to recent reports, the use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the tech giant, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in looks with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the manufacturer noted in the lawsuit.

Recent findings suggest that CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the manufacturer estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 initiative year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene mentioned.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company said in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment stated in the lawsuit.

It has been revealed that the company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

It has been revealed that "Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the organization mentioned. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in looks with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the tech giant tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, mentioned that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment said in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the tech giant said.

Seabed Mining Has a Refinery Problem Worth Billions

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Metals Company wants to recover polymetallic nodules from the seabed and sell the nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese they contain.
  • It has been revealed that that gap belongs in the mining economics.
  • According to recent reports, offshore collection gets the attention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Metals Company wants to recover polymetallic nodules from the seabed and sell the nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese they contain. That business needs an industrial processing system before its revenue projections become sales. TMC’s November 2026 enhancement exposed the timing problem. Its proposed refinery complex in Brownsville, Texas, may not be operating when offshore collection begins. An established Japanese smelter operated by Pacific Metals, or PAMCO, is the prospective initial route, but it needs modifications to accept commercial volumes of nodules.

It has been revealed that that gap belongs in the mining economics. TMC’s 2025 prefeasibility study allocated $4.426 billion to two proposed US hydrometallurgical refineries, about 89% of the study’s $4.971 billion of initial project capital. The denominator has a particular financing structure: the offshore amount covers the first collection system after an Allseas capital credit, while later systems are to be supplied through contracts and paid for through operating costs. The newer Brownsville proposal also has a different industrial scope. The 2025 figure shows the size of the processing business TMC’s economics must support, not a completed financing commitment for Brownsville.

According to recent reports, offshore collection gets the attention. Refineries decide what saleable material a collection system produces and who captures its value. A nodule delivered to port is a complex mineral feedstock, not a sale of four finished metals. One processing route smelts nodules into a nickel-copper-cobalt alloy and manganese silicate, converts the alloy into matte and refines the matte into marketable metals or chemicals. The manganese product needs customers or additional treatment. Each step consumes capital, energy, reagents, skilled labor and working capital.

Recent findings suggest that TMC has a meaningful metallurgical program. Its third-quarter 2026 SEC filing describes earlier North American tests of about 70 tons of nodules and a 2,000-ton industrial demonstration at PAMCO’s Hachinohe facility. Further work at SGS in Canada tested the refining of intermediate material into battery-grade products. PAMCO has completed feasibility work on treating roughly 1.3 million wet tons per year through a modified existing facility. That is a stronger starting point than a conceptual processing flowsheet.

The November 12 corporate update nevertheless put the industrial dependency in plain view. TMC’s preferred Brownsville facility will be difficult to complete before the first commercial nodules arrive, and the Japanese facility requires modifications and aligned schedules. Korea Zinc, Glencore, Hatch, Mariana Minerals and other partners provide useful expertise and commercial relationships. Those relationships still leave the construction, commissioning, financing and refining arrangements to complete.

According to recent reports, the value gap matters as much as the capital bill. In our 2025 seabed mining techno-economic assessment, metallurgist Lyle Trytten and I calculated a $553-per-ton contained-component reference value for representative Clarion-Clipperton Zone nodules at fixed historical metal prices. Using estimated purchase terms informed by analogous mineral markets, the same assessment gave a modeled raw-feed value of $188–256 per ton, or about 34–46% of that contained reference value.

The gap pays for real industrial work. Processors bear metal recovery losses, treatment costs, plant capital, financing, product quality and operating risk, and they need a return. The values are estimates on a common reference basis, not bids from refineries or the profit a processor would pocket. Commercial nodule tonnage is often reported wet; TMC’s study assumes 28% moisture. Feed-price comparisons with wet-ton mine costs require the same mass basis.

Industry observers note that the mining company has three main choices. It can sell the raw nodules at a price a processor can afford. It can keep title to the material and pay a plant to process it, provided the contract sets capacity, treatment charges, recoveries and risk allocation. Or it can finance and operate refining facilities and pursue a larger portion of the finished-metal revenue. None transfers the work, capital and risk out of the industrial system.

TMC’s own operating estimates reinforce that point. The 2025 study projected $13.622 billion of lifetime processing costs and $3.254 billion of refining costs, together about $103 per wet ton, or 42% of its modeled operating expenditure. Those costs sit alongside the proposed refinery capital. The production system may be offshore, but the economic center of gravity reaches well into the onshore industrial chain.

In a recent development, impossible Metals has a different, less developed processing position. Its published strategy begins with outsourcing to modified plants in allied countries and envisions dedicated facilities later. Its economic model used approximately $791 per ton of contained-metal value under its selected prices and grades, deducted a $230 processing charge, and arrived at roughly $560 per ton delivered to port. Those numbers use different input assumptions from our assessment and cannot be treated as a direct comparison with the $188–256 estimate. The commercial question is whether a processor would accept the feedstock and the risks on the terms in Impossible Metals’ model.

According to recent reports, existing nickel-processing projects offer warning enough. Ravensthorpe, Goro and Ambatovy had familiar metallurgical technologies yet encountered expensive commissioning and operational difficulties. An unusual feedstock, high-volume throughput, uncertain manganese outlets and synchronized offshore and onshore ramp-up add challenges for nodule ventures. Demonstrating that the chemistry works settles only one part of the investment case.

TMC has considerably more testing and more developed partners than Impossible Metals. That distinction matters. Neither has demonstrated a fully operating processing chain that delivers the required metals at its intended scale, recovery, capital cost and commercial terms. Government financing could change who carries part of the risk, but not what must be built or operated.

In a recent development, A seabed mining firm cannot book finished-metal economics while making the refinery somebody else’s problem. Investors, taxpayers and prospective processing partners need to know who provides the billions in capital, who carries the ramp-up risk and how much of the metal value the collector retains after every participant has been paid.

Recent findings suggest that my full TFIE Strategy Briefing article follows the processing alternatives, TMC’s Japanese and US aims, Impossible Metals’ outsourcing assumptions, and the resulting revenue and investment gaps. It is the third article in a five-part seabed mining assessment.

#133788. A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1404 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising newly introduced way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to newly introduced treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
  • In a recent development, the discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising newly introduced way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to newly introduced treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

In a recent development, the discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's.

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," mentioned Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease.".

To investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage.

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

Recent findings suggest that one crucial effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

According to recent reports, the protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," stated Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see.".

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse.

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

According to recent reports, SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

Recent findings suggest that the results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," mentioned Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies.".

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an notable protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments.

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

Sources indicate that they combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis demonstrated that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

The researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," mentioned Huijie Huang.

It has been revealed that plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies.".

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research.

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

The team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

According to recent reports, "Mouse cells and human cells are different," mentioned Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment.".

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Industry observers note that ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal newly introduced treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.
