📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” takes place in the Theranos founder’s former Del Mar, CA, rental—and the property’s location in an exclusive, gated community could be just part of the reason the film’s unexpected release was such a smash.

Industry observers note that the project—which is now available to stream on demand and was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim—was kept secret for the four years it was in production, leaving viewers in awe after the documentary’s surprise Sept. 6 premiere at Telluride Film Festival.

Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, invited the film crew—which Oppenheim told Variety was intentionally kept intimate to keep the project a secret—to reside in the guesthouse of the home for the 34 days before she reported to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023.

“Keeping it under wraps was very key because we never wanted to get in front of what we were capturing,” the director shared.

The crew would typically shoot for 16-hour days, with Fielder telling Variety that cameras were strategically positioned to “cover the whole house” so nothing would be missed.

The four-bedroom, four-bathroom beachfront property is located in an ultraprivate community less than a half-hour from San Diego. Called Sandy Lane, it features just about a dozen residences.

It has been revealed that “This is basically a hidden community. It’s a guard-gated community, which is so rare on a beach, which is why you have a lot of high-profile individuals up and down this strip,” celebrity real estate agent Josh Altman explained in a home tour of another property on the community’s sole street.

Given the home's private location—and considering California’s anti-paparazzi legislation protecting private property from capture—it’s plain to see why Holmes and Evans opted to rent the 2,200-square-foot dwelling in the time leading up to her imprisonment.

The Fresh York Times also previously reported that the couple and their two children moved to the area to be nearer to Evans’ family. His parents, William L. Evans and Susan Evans, are the hotel magnates behind Evans Hotels, a San Diego–based hospitality firm.

Although the property is currently off-market, a previous listing indicates the single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to the private beach.

As seen in the film, the abode features tall ceilings with exposed-beams and sizable windows connecting the home to the serene surrounding landscape. Midcentury modern design is present throughout the home, which is paneled in honey-hued wood.

While Realtor.com® estimates the property’s current market value to be about $5.8 million, it’s unclear just how much Holmes and Evans shelled out to reside there temporarily. The most recent publicly listed rent was $5,650 a month in 2015, which is a decrease from the $5,950 rent it was listed for in 2012.

Industry observers note that the Sandy Lane spot is not the only prominent rental property Holmes has retreated to since her legal troubles began. During her trial from Aug. 31, 2021, to Jan. 3, 2022, she resided in one of the seven homes of San Francisco’s notable Green Gables.

The sprawling 74-acre property was owned by the Fleishhacker family for over a century before it was sold for a record-breaking $85 million in 2025.

Before Theranos came crumbling down, Holmes and her former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, purchased a $9 million French provincial manor in Atherton, a wealthy enclave of Silicon Valley.

Privacy was likely a factor in that decision, as well, as the five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom mansion was set behind a gated entrance and tall trees.

The home was considerably more lavish than the beach bungalow that serves as the backdrop for “You Can See Everything,” with a 6,800-square-foot main home accompanied by gardens, a pool, and a pavilion on a 1.16-acre lot.

Along with the couple’s young children, Evans has since relocated from California to Texas, so the family can visit Holmes in prison, where she is serving an 11-year sentence for three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The sentence was reduced to nine years for good behavior, and Holmes has since been approved for placement in a community correction center, ABC News reported, citing an update from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System.

Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in De Valle, TX, in August 2027.

It has been revealed that the Virginia Department of Health announced on Nov. 20 its first measles-associated death since 1978.

According to recent reports, the individual was a child younger than four years of age who had tested positive for measles, though the state has refrained from providing more information about the case for privacy reasons. The state has reported 220 cases in total this year, as of a Nov. 19 dashboard update, with most occurring in its central region and at least 179 of which were confirmed to be unvaccinated.

It is the fourth state this year to have reported a measles-associated death, following Pennsylvania, where a ninth death was reported on Monday, as well as New York and Wisconsin. Pennsylvania's health department noted it has now confirmed 1,638 cases across 46 of its counties this year, and noted that only five of those were among individuals vaccinated against the disease.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of a Nov. 19 update, lists 5,838 confirmed cases of measles this year, well above 2025's total of 2,289. The agency has recognized six of the reported deaths as compared to states' 13, as the federal body said it is looking to develop a standardized definition for deaths due to measles amid disputes over the use and reporting of "measles-associated" deaths.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

According to recent reports, the status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. (Editor's note: The public health body made its official announcement on Nov. 17).

In a recent development, the U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action plan that includes immunization and surveillance.

The decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 upgrade from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

In a recent development, health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

According to recent reports, "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is vital for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.".

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone remarked they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

The Upcoming York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, Newly introduced York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease.".

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone noted they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a upcoming standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

Sources indicate that A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to Newly introduced York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they stated.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a latest, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

In a recent development, the CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

Latest Update: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life.
  • It has been revealed that most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time.
  • Sources indicate that among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life. The discovery, made by researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC), could help doctors identify families with a heightened genetic risk and detect cancer before it spreads.

It has been revealed that most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time. However, approximately 5% to 10% are associated with inherited mutations that can be passed from parents to their children, creating a cancer risk that may extend across generations.

Sources indicate that among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These inherited changes can substantially raise the likelihood of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Testing for BRCA mutations has reshaped cancer prevention and treatment by allowing people with elevated risks to receive earlier screening and preventive care.

In a recent development, now, a study published in Cancer Discovery points to another gene, CDK12, as a potentially notable marker of inherited prostate cancer risk. After examining genetic information from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, the researchers discovered five unrelated men with inherited mutations in CDK12. Every one of these men developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62, meaning the cancer had spread beyond the prostate.

In a recent development, "What's striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed," said senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences in the UBC faculty of medicine and UBC President's Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. "The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options.".

A Hidden Genetic Cause of Aggressive Prostate Cancer.

The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about CDK12. Scientists previously believed that harmful changes in this gene developed spontaneously inside cancer cells rather than being inherited from a parent.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate whether the inherited mutations were actually contributing to the disease, the team examined the patients' tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic damage associated with loss of CDK12 function. This molecular fingerprint helped connect the inherited mutations to the development of their cancers.

In a recent development, "The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12," mentioned lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. "It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer.".

The findings emerged from a broad international research effort involving UBC, BC Cancer, the Vancouver Coastal Health Research Institute, and the University of Washington, along with scientists at institutions in Australia, the Netherlands, Spain, and Belgium.

Industry observers note that despite the potentially serious consequences, inherited CDK12 mutations appear to be exceptionally uncommon. The researchers found them in approximately one out of every 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer. Even at that low frequency, they estimate that hundreds of families around the world could be affected.

"While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it," said Dr. Tolmeijer. "Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads.".

Genetic Testing Could Help Detect Prostate Cancer Earlier.

One of the most promising implications of the discovery is that doctors may not need to develop entirely fresh testing technology to put the findings into practice.

It has been revealed that the researchers recommend including CDK12 in standard genetic testing panels used to assess hereditary prostate cancer risk. These panels examine multiple genes associated with inherited cancer susceptibility, helping identify individuals who may benefit from closer medical monitoring.

It has been revealed that importantly, the clinical technology required to detect CDK12 mutations already exists. That could make expanding genetic testing relatively straightforward, potentially reducing the time and expense needed to bring the discovery into routine patient care.

According to recent reports, "One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it," said Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. "Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more quickly.".

Could the Same Mutation Increase Ovarian Cancer Risk?

The study also uncovered clues suggesting that inherited CDK12 mutations might be associated with ovarian cancer, although more research is needed to establish whether they increase the risk.

Several of the men with inherited CDK12 mutations had relatives with a history of ovarian cancer. The investigators also identified another person who had ovarian cancer and carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. Analysis of that person's tumor revealed the same characteristic genetic signature seen in the prostate cancer cases.

Together, these observations suggest that CDK12 could potentially play a role in hereditary cancer risk beyond the prostate. Further studies will be needed to determine how strongly the mutations are associated with ovarian cancer and whether they should influence screening recommendations.

For families carrying these rare mutations, the potential benefits of identifying their genetic risk could be substantial. Earlier testing may give relatives the opportunity to receive closer surveillance and, if cancer develops, begin treatment before it reaches an advanced stage.

"With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer," noted Dr. Wyatt.

The research received funding from the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Terry Fox Research Institute, Canadian Cancer Society, Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Michael Smith Health Research BC, U.S. National Institutes of Health, BC Cancer Foundation, and other funding partners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Army plans to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.

According to recent reports, the U.S. army has detonated 9,7000 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday after warning that the bomb-making chemicals had degraded and could be explosive.

The controlled detonated of the country's entire stockpile of the explosive was carried out at at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, IA at 10am EST.

After the detonation, local news station KWQC reported seeing a large plume of smoke.

Recent findings suggest that gov. Kim Reynolds said the detonation was a success.

“I want to commend Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, Army leadership, and the skilled soldiers who planned and executed a flawless detonation this morning at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and express my gratitude to the Trump Administration for its whole-of-government response," she said.

The detonation came after a lawsuit was filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter asking the federal appeals court to halt the plan.

Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the plans were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization.

Industry observers note that set to be detonated are 68 drums of degraded lead azide, adding up to roughly 9,700 pounds, which have become sensitive and unstable. It is the primary explosive used to initiate munitions.

A controlled detonation is now the only viable option, according to the Army’s Q&A page about the event.

As lead azide degrades, it crystalizes and becomes sensitive to temperature changes, shock, and friction, making it unsafe to move. There are chemical neutralization procedures, but the drums are too unstable for the physical manipulation this option requires, according to the Army.

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7 Director Jim Macy wrote a letter to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, ensuring her that the EPA was working alongside the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Defense to ensure the controlled detonation was “conducted in the safest manner possible.”.

“All agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” Macy wrote in the letter, according to the Iowa Capital Dispatch.

An updated public safety advisory shared by the Army on Tuesday shared the agency’s aims to make the detonation as safe as possible. The lead azide will be detonated in earth-covered magazines, which are built for the purposes of holding ammunition and explosives, and are reinforced.

Industry observers note that additional physical barriers made of sand, a “water wall,” gel blocks, and aqueous foam barriers will be in place to contain particle dispersion, absorb thermal energy, and reduce airborne particulate dispersal. These measures, as well as drone surveillance of lead levels, are in place to track and minimize deposition outside the plant.

In a recent development, the Army has acknowledged that lead particles will impact communities outside the plant. It has defined an evacuation zone as a "5-mile cone extending southwest of IAAAP.".

Those in the evacuation zone will be provided short-term hotel lodging, food, water, and transportation as needed.

It has also laid out recommendations for those outside the evacuation zone, such as sheltering in place, closing all windows and doors, and setting heating to recirculate and avoid pulling in air from outside.

Still, environmental groups are concerned about the lead plume, which they say could spread 100 miles, depending on weather conditions.

"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," stated Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, in a press release shared with Realtor.com®.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal.".

Recent findings suggest that the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, Iowa Chapter, were only made aware of the unprecedented detonation plan early last week, initially scheduled for Friday. In response, the groups filed a lawsuit on Thursday challenging the permit that the EPA issued the Army.

“Based on the information that was made public at the time, which was very little information, there were serious concerns about the effectiveness of the public notification and the information being put out to protect the public,” Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earth Justice, tells Realtor.com.

“There were serious concerns about the mitigations measures in place to reduce the impact as well as to properly do remediation and cleanup and address any harm that people may face from the impact of the detonation.”.

Many local lawmakers were not made aware of the controlled detonation either, and were only informed about the plans and risk once the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra club told them, despite the widespread impact on surrounding communities, according to Chau.

“That’s why we filed the lawsuit: to make sure that all the information and resources and capabilities that could be provided were provided to the people potentially impacted by this,” claims Chau.

“Since that filing, a lot of things have happened. The government has put out a lot more information, and while we expect a detonation to take place this Wednesday, we are glad to see that because there was additional time, there are now additional mitigation measures and resources have been provided for potentially impacted people.”.

It has been revealed that the Department of Justice responded in opposition to the lawsuit. Both the DOJ and Army maintain that a controlled detonation is the safest option and further delay, especially with cold weather approaching, could lead to a natural, uncontrolled detonation, which would be more difficult to mitigate.

“The Army has delayed detonation by three days now,” the DOJ’s brief said. “But every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit.”.

Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has launched a upcoming online portal for payers, providers and other stakeholders to manage and monitor disputes under the federal Independent Dispute Resolution process.

Sources indicate that the IDR Gateway went online Nov. 13 and was officially unveiled Nov. 20. It replaces the web forms parties previously used to manage disputes, most of which will no longer be available outside of the centralized platform after Jan. 15, 2027, per a government fact sheet.

According to recent reports, payers will eventually be required to register on IDR Gateway so that it is easier for providers to identify the correct party, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said earlier this year when finalizing an overhaul of No Surprises Act protocols. That registration feature will be added “in the future on a rolling basis,” CMS said last week, with others like in-portal negotiation similarly rolling out over time “to improve accountability and reduce unnecessary filings,” the agency said last spring.

For now, the IDR Gateway allows parties and their representatives to initiate a dispute, respond to proposed selections of IDR entities and submit a payment offer. Its other tools allow owners to view, search, set up notifications and broadly analyze open disputes for their organization; an IDR Gateway Dashboard, CMS noted, offers a color-coded donut chart breaking down an organization’s different types of open disputes by phase, while another tool can generate detailed reports of dispute line items.

The administration also touted security measures inherent to the new portal. These include a new sign-up process that requires users to verify their identity with an approved credential service provider, and other protocols like a terms and conditions agreement that notes that unauthorized users could be subject to criminal prosecution.

The baseball-style IDR process enacted under the No Surprises Act, intended to handle out-of-network billing disputes away from the patient’s purview, has become a point of contention amid dispute volumes and payouts well beyond legislators’ expectations.

Arbitrators’ decisions have largely favored providers over payers (85% of decisions went toward providers last year), which alongside court decisions that tweaked CMS’ processes further toward provider preferences, has triggered outright condemnation from payers who have turned to lawsuits, restrictive policies and lobbying in a bit to reform the process. Recent analyses have pegged the IDR process’ impact for employer prepares at $8.4 billion in 2025 and total costs associated with the process at $22 billion for that same year.

Lawmakers including the No Surprises Act’s chief authors have said they hope to pass new legislation to fix or fully replace the IDR process, with December’s must-pass budget bill now looking like a likely vehicle for such a change.

A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder.
  • It has been revealed that the condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening.
  • It has been revealed that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder. Now, researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have uncovered evidence that challenges 30 years of established thinking and could open the door to a fresh treatment.

It has been revealed that the condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening. A fresh study published in Immunity identifies a previously underrecognized problem involving natural killer (NK) cells, immune cells that normally help the body eliminate infected cells.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur. The discovery also points to a possible treatment using existing medications called JAK inhibitors, which could be particularly valuable for patients who do not respond to current therapies.

In a recent development, "This study has revealed a fresh target for this inflammatory disorder and sets the scene for future clinical studies to explore the use of JAK inhibitors or other drugs to neutralize interferon gamma in patients with MKD," notes Professor Mike Rogers, Lab Head at Garvan and senior author of the study. "This could lead to a targeted treatment that hasn't been tried before.".

Why a Rare Immune Disease Causes Dangerous Inflammation.

Sources indicate that MKD is a lifelong condition known to affect hundreds of children and adults around the world, although researchers suspect that many people with the disorder have never been diagnosed. Patients experience recurring attacks of high fever, skin rashes, joint pain, and inflammation in the abdomen. The most serious episodes can cause potentially fatal complications.

According to recent reports, for roughly three decades, research into the disease has largely centered on macrophages, immune cells that help coordinate the body's inflammatory defenses. Existing treatments are designed to block an inflammatory signal released by these cells. However, approximately half of patients do not respond adequately, leaving a major need for better treatment options.

To investigate what might be missing from the prevailing explanation, the Garvan team examined blood samples from people with MKD and studied preclinical models of the disorder.

Their experiments revealed a significant defect in natural killer cells, which play an important role in the body's early defenses against viral infections. In MKD, these cells fail to mature properly and struggle to perform one of their most important functions: destroying infected cells before an infection can spread.

In a recent development, the consequences go beyond an impaired ability to fight infection. When natural killer cells cannot eliminate their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, activating other parts of the immune system and potentially triggering widespread inflammation.

"We found that these immune cells are essentially misfiring," explains Professor Rogers. "NK cells are loaded with toxic ammunition, stored in granules that are released to kill infected cells. However, in MKD these toxic granules can't be released from NK cells and remain trapped inside. When an NK cell fails to kill its target, it compensates by shouting for help, pumping out large amounts of interferon gamma - a powerful inflammatory signal. This activates other immune cells and causes the dangerous fever and widespread inflammation seen in patients.".

Discovery Challenges 30 Years of Immune Disease Research.

The findings suggest that natural killer cell dysfunction, rather than macrophage activity alone, plays a central role in driving MKD.

Dr. Marcia Munoz, Group Leader in the Rogers Lab and lead researcher on the study, says the results represent a major change in how scientists understand the disease.

"This really turns on its head 30 years of dogma about what was thought to be the underlying mechanism of disease. In MKD, the primary problem is in NK cells and not in macrophages, as previously believed," she states.

To investigate how this cellular defect contributes to the disorder, the Garvan researchers collaborated with Professor Mariapia Degli-Esposti and scientists at Monash University.

Using preclinical models, the team established a connection between malfunctioning natural killer cells and the severe symptoms associated with MKD. Their experiments showed that when the immune system cannot clear a viral infection, the resulting inflammatory response can cause extensive damage to organs.

These results help explain why a disorder involving defective immune defenses can also produce episodes of extreme inflammation.

Existing Drug Shows Promise for a New Treatment.

The discovery has already helped guide an experimental treatment approach for a severely affected infant.

Working with doctors at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, the researchers explored whether baricitinib could reduce the excessive inflammatory signaling associated with MKD.

Baricitinib belongs to a class of medications known as JAK inhibitors. These drugs interfere with signaling pathways used by the immune system, including those involved in responses to interferon gamma. The medication is already used to treat other immune-related conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and eczema.

It has been revealed that doctors added baricitinib to the infant's existing treatment regimen and subsequently observed an improvement in the child's condition. Inflammatory flare-ups became less frequent, and severe inflammation affecting the gastrointestinal tract began to heal.

Although the results from a single patient cannot establish whether the treatment will work more broadly, the improvement provides encouraging early evidence for a strategy that targets a different part of the inflammatory process.

The researchers believe their findings provide a foundation for future clinical studies investigating JAK inhibitors and other medications that block interferon gamma activity in patients with MKD, particularly those who have not benefited from standard treatments.

Discovery Could Help Explain Other Genetic Diseases.

The potential implications extend beyond MKD itself.

Researchers have introduced the term 'prenylopathies' to describe a family of genetic disorders involving the same metabolic pathway affected in MKD. Early findings suggest that these related diseases may share a similar underlying problem involving natural killer cells that fail to function properly and instead generate excessive inflammatory signals.

If further studies confirm this connection, scientists may be able to identify common disease mechanisms and develop more targeted approaches to diagnosis and treatment across multiple disorders.

"Confirming this link could help end the diagnostic odyssey many patients endure for years or even decades before receiving effective treatment," notes Professor Rogers.

Sources indicate that professor Mike Rogers is a Conjoint Professor at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney. Dr. Marcia Munoz is a Conjoint Senior Lecturer at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney.

Microsoft declares internal Code Red after nearly 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that microsoft Corp.
  • Industry observers note that the outage on Nov.
  • In a memo to staff on Friday, Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, described the outage as the most customer-affecting incident in the history of Exchange Online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:44 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

It has been revealed that microsoft Corp. has declared an internal “Code Red” to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures following the nearly 24-hour outage that took down Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services earlier this month, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters today.

Industry observers note that the outage on Nov. 12 and 13 also disrupted Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence assistant, affecting governments from Australia and Japan to the U.S., delaying trading firms and disrupting airline communications. The designation signals the most severe and urgent level of alert inside Microsoft, according to the report.

In a memo to staff on Friday, Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, described the outage as the most customer-affecting incident in the history of Exchange Online. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote. He also conceded that the work done over the years had not been enough to protect the firm on the day of the outage.

In a recent development, engineers working the incident faced a “fog of war,” according to a separate memo sent on Monday by Amanda Silver, corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ. Silver’s memo describes responders exchanging more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, with diagnostic data spread across fragmented internal tracking systems.

The Code Red covers five workstreams set out by Silver, including load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft has also set a target of resolving future incidents worldwide within an hour, with AI agents to be used to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly.

How long it takes to push out fixes is another issue raised by Henderson. Writing in an earlier memo this month, Henderson noted one urgent production fix had taken five to six days to reach worldwide saturation, while for urgent security concerns the goal is to go from detection to safe worldwide deployment within an hour, something he admitted the company has yet to achieve. Henderson also aims to hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team that oversees the engineering group responsible for the underlying Microsoft 365 services, along with weekly reviews of the corrective work.

The outage itself was blamed by Microsoft on a defect introduced in July in a fix that had been prepared for its Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Under certain load conditions, lock contention inside an internal Windows process was found to exhaust processor and memory resources on the servers, leaving more than 80% of them unresponsive at the worst point, according to Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report. Microsoft, whose Chief Executive Satya Nadella has publicly apologized for the disruption, has stated the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents.

Silver’s memo also cites Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, who told a Code Red review that the affected component had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”.

Speed comes with its own risks, according to security experts. “What concerns me is that speed and safety pull against each other,” Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at AI security operations startup Secure.com, told SiliconANGLE. In his view, a pipeline able to push a fix to the world in an hour “can push a mistake in an hour.”.

Geographic traffic partitioning, which Ahmed said limits how far a single bad change can travel, is the one of the five Code Red workstreams he would be watching.

Darin Fredde, senior director and offensive security evangelist at autonomous penetration testing company Ridge Security Technology Inc., noted that “an organization may have a recovery strategy but still struggle to execute it if the tools needed to recover depend on the service that has failed.”.

If the AI Bubble Pops, Here’s What It Means for Your Home’s Value

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When artificial intelligence giant Anthropic went public last week, its $1.494 trillion valuation exceeded the combined value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metropolitan area, according to research from Realtor.com®.
  • Less than a week later, the company's shares fell below their IPO price, as a renewed sell-off in tech stocks stoked fears that the AI bubble may already be bursting.
  • “This is how the exuberance ends—not with a whimper but with a bang,” Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote on Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When artificial intelligence giant Anthropic went public last week, its $1.494 trillion valuation exceeded the combined value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metropolitan area, according to research from Realtor.com®.

Less than a week later, the company's shares fell below their IPO price, as a renewed sell-off in tech stocks stoked fears that the AI bubble may already be bursting.

“This is how the exuberance ends—not with a whimper but with a bang,” Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote on Monday.

Krugman, who warned of America's housing bubble as early as 2005, acknowledges he's less certain about AI valuations than he was about home prices two decades ago. But earlier this month, he warned that an AI bust would almost certainly trigger a recession, potentially more painful than the one that followed the dot-com crash.

Others on Wall Street aren't so sure. Many investors remain confident in the industry's fundamentals and see the sell-off as a necessary correction rather than the end of the boom.

But after years of a bull market powered by a handful of AI darlings, newly introduced research from Realtor.com finds evidence that the resulting fortunes have helped shape some of America’s most expensive housing markets.

Now, a reversal of those gains could threaten a source of wealth far more central to the financial lives of middle-class Americans: their homes.

Anthropic's IPO alone was expected to mint around 2,800 millionaires among its current and former employees, according to estimates from private-market research firm Sacra reported by Reuters.

In a recent development, but Americans needn't work in AI or invest in individual tech stocks to have shared in the windfall. Between the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 and Nov. 3 of this year, the S&P 500 gained nearly $32 trillion in market value—more than half of which came from just 10 AI-linked companies, according to Bloomberg.

Sources indicate that about 62% of Americans own stocks, either directly or through investments such as retirement accounts, according to a 2025 Gallup poll. Yet the wealthiest 10% of households hold 88% of the country's household stocks and mutual fund assets.

In the San Francisco Bay Area's AI hubs, some of that AI-powered stock wealth has translated into an estimated $61,180 in additional down payment on a typical home, according to research from Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu. At the entry-level luxury tier, that premium reached nearly $200,000 in 2025.

The extra cash these buyers have brought to the market has allowed them to bid higher without taking on more debt, potentially displacing competitors into less expensive price brackets and driving up competition further down the market, Xu's earlier research suggests.

And so, what’s a barrier to entry for prospective buyers becomes a source of equity gains for existing homeowners—even those who have never invested in AI.

Annual home price growth now exceeds the national rate in all three markets where Xu identified signs of AI wealth bolstering down payments: Chicago (6.9%), Latest York City (5.8%), and San Francisco (3.7%), compared with 2.1% nationally, according to Tuesday's Case-Shiller release.

It’s an especially crucial point to make here because real estate wealth is more widely distributed than stock. Households between the 50th and 90th wealth percentiles hold nearly half of the country's household real estate assets, but just 11.4% of its stocks and mutual fund shares, according to second-quarter Federal Reserve data.

Homeowners in markets buoyed by AI wealth have, in effect, acquired a stake in the industry's stock market performance—whether or not they own any shares.

Industry observers note that and the potential losses are enormous. To gauge their scale, Krugman looks to the so-called Buffett indicator, which measures the total value of U.S. stocks relative to the country's gross domestic product.

Industry observers note that before the recent sell-off, the ratio had climbed well above its peak during the dot-com bubble. AI-related companies accounted for nearly half of the S&P 500's market value and drove most of the increase in the indicator over the past several years, Krugman explains.

“If the Buffett indicator falls back to what it was in, say, 2019, that would wipe out wealth equal to around 80 percent of GDP: $25 trillion,” he wrote.

And if his warning seems alarmist, consider what he wrote about the U.S. housing market in August 2005: “This is the way the bubble ends: not with a pop, but with a hiss.”.

More than two years before the onset of the Great Recession, Krugman identified falling sales and rising inventory as the early signs of a housing bust, as sellers struggled to command prices that buyers were no longer willing to pay.

Some of those symptoms are present today. In October, contract signings fell 17% annually while inventory grew 7.4%. Asking prices recorded their 12th consecutive month of annual declines, according to Realtor.com research.

In a recent development, but the slowdown predates November's sell-off. Elevated mortgage rates and years of home price growth that outpaced wages have driven buyers to the sidelines, while many homeowners can afford to wait for better offers.

“On the seller side, we see more of a pause than an exodus,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, noted earlier this month.

The question is whether an AI bust would produce another localized housing correction or a national downturn.

Recent findings suggest that “Generally speaking, the stock market and housing market can be connected, but usually not directly,” Krimmel explained amid an earlier bout of AI stock volatility in November 2025. “If they're moving together, that's typically because of some other outside force (could be driven by policy, Fed moves, and credit conditions, or a large macro shock) and/or because of changes in the job market.”.

Industry observers note that to his point, when the dot-com bubble burst, the Nasdaq plunged more than 75% from its peak, wiping out trillions in paper wealth. Yet national home values continued to climb through the 2001 recession.

In San Francisco, however, home values fell 6.1% between February 2001 and January 2002, even as they rose 6% nationally, according to an analysis of seasonally adjusted Case-Shiller home price data.

The bigger question hanging over the housing market, though, is what an AI bust would mean for household spending.

When households lose stock market wealth, they tend to spend less, even if their paychecks haven't changed—a phenomenon economists call the wealth effect. And just as stock market gains have held up demand for homes, they've also helped sustain demand elsewhere in the economy.

Any resulting pullback in spending, therefore, could end up rippling into layoffs in industries far removed from AI. Likewise, a slowdown in AI infrastructure investment could compound those losses, jeopardizing construction and manufacturing jobs in communities distant from Silicon Valley.

“Labor market softness is key for aggregate (and housing) demand,” Krimmel stated last year.

And while the destruction of stock market wealth might initially dampen housing demand in a handful of affluent markets, rising unemployment could weaken it nationwide.

Industry observers note that during the dot-com bust, the Federal Reserve cut interest rates aggressively, helping sustain housing demand despite the economic downturn. Persistent inflation could complicate a similar response today.

“Lower interest rates will, in theory, help struggling companies' finances and allow them to keep existing workers, hire more, and/or provide pay raises to top performers,” Krimmel explained last November.

It has been revealed that access to credit could also become a problem. Tech companies are relying more heavily on corporate debt and private credit to finance their expansion, according to the European Central Bank's November Financial Stability Review. Losses on those investments could prompt lenders to tighten credit, making financing harder to obtain for homebuyers and builders alike.

The combination of falling incomes and more restrictive lending could depress home values in markets where AI wealth never drove them up in the first place.

But unlike during the Great Recession, a decline in home values would leave far fewer homeowners owing more than their properties are worth, limiting the risk of widespread foreclosures and the additional downward pressure on prices that forced sales can create.

Industry observers note that “The typical homeowner today—and the housing market overall—is still well-positioned to withstand a correction without it turning into a crisis,” Krimmel mentioned last November. “Home equity hit an all-time high in 2025Q2; mortgage holders are largely locked into sub-4% rates, giving them lower payments that are increasingly being eaten away by inflation. Very few homeowners are at risk of going underwater, even if prices were to decline 10% to 15%.”.

A year later, homeowner equity cushions remain substantial and mortgage delinquencies are low by historical standards, according to the Fed's November Financial Stability Report.

Sources indicate that “Obviously, [a stock market crash] is not something anyone wants to see play out, and undoubtedly, if a stock market correction spilled over into the housing market, many homeowners would feel the pain,” Krimmel noted. “The silver lining of that hypothetical is that the knock-on effects would not be as severe. Luckily, the history of the housing bust and Great Recession would not repeat itself.”.

In a recent development, but for tens of millions of families, home equity is the college fund, the retirement strategy, the safety net, and the most vital source of wealth they'll ever build. The financial protections that could keep them in their homes during a downturn wouldn't necessarily protect that wealth.

Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dozens of academic health system and teaching hospital chief executives are turning to Congress in a bid to blunt a controversial subsidy cut coming to Medicare Part B in the new year.

Earlier this month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services locked in intends to reduce reimbursements for outpatient drugs dispensed by participants in the 340B Drug Pricing Program during the 2027 calendar year.

Sources indicate that specifically, the agency noted it will move from the current rate of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% down to ASP minus 28%, with a corresponding 7.5% increase in non-drug outpatient payments to maintain budget neutrality. CMS said the change will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by an estimated $4.35 billion and drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion during the policy’s first year.

Hospital groups—particularly those that chiefly represent nonprofit or safety-net hospitals—have denounced the blueprint’s disproportionate effect on hospitals participating in the decades-old subsidy program, as well as a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate but will benefit from the budget-neutral offset.

With their formal opposition to the policy’s proposal set aside by CMS, 95 executives whose organizations are members of the Association of American Medical Colleges have now penned a letter to leaders of the House and the Senate pleading for a two-year delay to the rate cut’s implementation.

“This policy will exacerbate already negative Medicare margins at a time when teaching hospitals are already grappling with rising financial challenges resulting from inflation, workforce shortages, manufacturer-driven restrictions on the 340B program and an expected rise in uncompensated care costs,” they wrote.

Industry observers note that the executives acknowledged that the final policy’s rate of ASP minus 28% is “slightly smaller” than CMS’ initial proposal of ASP minus 33.4%, but said the change was still a threat to the country’s healthcare safety net. They noted the cuts represent a nearly $5.5 billion reduction that would be disproportionately shouldered by AAMC-member teaching hospitals—who comprise 17% of all impacted hospitals—but will see almost $3 billion of that total.

Sources indicate that those funds are necessary to finance critical care services at academic hospitals including trauma care, inpatient behavioral care, transplant surgery and labor and delivery, the signatories warned lawmakers. They also noted that their institutions are major referral hubs that accept “the most complex transfer cases from lower acuity settings, such as rural and community hospitals,” in a way that for-profit hospitals and others who will benefit from the final rule do not.

“While we understand that Congress has an interest in improving the 340B program, and are broadly supportive of meaningful transparency and accountability for covered entities, we also strongly believe that cutting Medicare payment to 340B hospitals is not the appropriate policy mechanism to achieve these goals,” they wrote. “Therefore, we respectfully request that you support a two-year delay in the [Outpatient Prospective Payment System] rule’s payment cuts for 340B-acquired drugs.”.

Among the letter’s 95 signatories were the heads of Cedars-Sinai, Stanford Health Care, Yale Upcoming Haven Health, Tampa General Hospital, Rush University System for Health, Mass General Brigham, Nebraska Medicine, RWJBarnabas Health, NewYork-Presbyterian, UNC Health and School of Medicine, OHSU, Jefferson Health, Penn Medicine, Vanderbilt Health and Froedtert ThedaCare.

In a recent development, the academic health systems and hospitals’ turn to lawmakers comes after their rebukes of CMS’ 340B policy have fallen on deaf ears. The agency and broader Trump administration have often sided with critics of the subsidy program on related initiatives like a pilot rebate program, citing 340B’s rapid growth and contribution to increased healthcare spending. A Health and Human Services Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation policy brief defending the rate cut made those views crystal clear with claims that the program has incentivized provider consolidation while doing little to serve patients’ needs.

Meanwhile, Congress, spurred by public pressure to reduce healthcare costs, has proposed its own legislative fixes to 340B. Though each bill aims to preserve the program and subsidize safety-net care, some are more friendly to the hospital industry than others.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As home prices and mortgage rates have climbed in recent years, homebuyers and developers alike have turned to factory-built tiny homes as a potential solution for affordable housing.

While low prices and fast shipping make prefab homes from Amazon look like a bargain, buyers should be aware of several factors with this purchase—starting with the fact that selling them is actually prohibited on the platform.

Amazon prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings, with its Seller Central policy explicitly banning complete prefab homes, tiny house kits marketed as living spaces, modular and container homes, and other factory-built housing units.

So, why then does a search for "prefab tiny homes" bring up thousands of results?

Many of the tiny homes on Amazon are simple backyard sheds, compliant with the retailer's rules. Others walk a fine line.

Several listings, which fall between $20,000 and $25,000, use words like “prefabricated steel building” and “expandable modular container.”.

The highlights for one now unlisted item described it as “a portable, multi-purpose outdoor structure for storage, workspace, display, or commercial utility use.” It goes on to say that it has “versatile non-residential use—suitable for office setup, equipment storage, pop-up workspace, site unit, studio, or backyard utility structure.”.

Nowhere in the description did it call itself a home or use words like "residential" or "habitation.".

Recent findings suggest that however, a flip through the photos demonstrated images of a warm and inviting interior—including a seemingly spacious bedroom. Potential layouts showed both one- and two-bedroom floor aims.

Realtor.com® reached out to Amazon for a comment on these listings but received no response.

Those looking to take the leap on a tiny home should still give local permitting requirements a close look. There is no single national zoning law for tiny homes in the United States, so buyers should check their local ordinances before purchasing.

For example, in Los Angeles, tiny homes on permanent foundations, rather than wheels, are generally allowed, but each habitable room must be at least 150 square feet under the California Residential Code. Units must also meet all building code requirements for habitable space, such as proper ventilation and fire safety.

As long as owners receive the proper install and permits, owners can generally take out insurance on tiny homes, whether they serve as a primary residence or accessory dwelling unit like a detached studio or office.

Sources indicate that “Insurance companies generally don't have issues with prefab homes, manufactured homes, or sheds. Most also don't have issues with an accessory dwelling unit on the site of a house,” Tom Firestine, founder of Longmeadow Insurance, tells Realtor.com. “When the local municipality allows them, we don’t have an issue extending coverage.”.

Regional weather differences raise distinct structural challenges for tiny homes. In Phoenix, extreme heat requires all units to have proper insulation and HVAC. While coastal regions contend with high winds, Firestine, who works out of Chicago, claims their main concern is heavy snow loads.

“The biggest concern is whether the structure's install is permitted and how the use is presented to the insurance tech giant,” says Firestine. “Intentionally misrepresenting something on an insurance application is the easiest way to get a claim denied. Insurers generally won't insure an illegal structure.”.

Voters expect lawmakers to address healthcare affordability, access: poll" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Half of voters stated they are paying more this year in premiums and out-of-pocket costs, according to a latest national poll.

Lake Research Partners and Bellwether Research & Consulting surveyed 1,000 voters between Oct. 20 and Oct. 28 on behalf of the National Health Council, and 50% stated their premiums and out-of-pocket costs are higher this year compared to last year. Among those with commercial insurance, 63% said their premiums have risen, and 60% said their out-of-pocket costs have grown year-over-year.

In addition, 25% of those surveyed noted they had a claim for a prescription denied, and 24% said they waited more than two weeks for a prior authorization decision. Twenty-one percent said that they struggled to find a specialist.

Healthcare costs and the broader economy were major factors in Democrats' significant victories in the latest midterm election. And the NHC poll finds that voters expect Congress to act on addressing the costs that they face.

Most of the surveyed voters (78%) remarked they believe that the healthcare system warrants major changes or a complete overhaul, and 84% said they would support a candidate that would make it a priority to reform the healthcare insurance system.

However, 74% of those surveyed rated the effort from elected officials to address affordability and access as either fair or poor.

It has been revealed that “Holding onto a proposal isn’t the same as being protected by it. Patients are watching their costs rise and their coverage change, and they’re worried about what that means for their families down the road,” stated Randall Rutta, CEO of the National Health Council, in an announcement. “The new Congress has a real opportunity to change that, and patients across the country will be watching.”.

The survey highlights a number of potential policies that would have broad voter support. For example, 91% of those surveyed said they would support eliminating surprise medical bills and policies to require price transparency.

Sources indicate that in addition, 90% mentioned they would back efforts to reduce out-of-pocket costs, while 89% said they favor requiring health aims to cover treatments that were prescribed by doctors. Eighty-eight percent support efforts to increase screening and early detection for medical risks.

"Voters aren't asking lawmakers to talk about health care differently," noted Christine Matthews, president of Bellwether Research and Consulting, in the release. "They want to see it work differently. Reform is a priority they expect the new Congress to deliver on.".

Tech Report: A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.
  • In a recent development, the research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac).
  • But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

In a recent development, the research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

It has been revealed that treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s key this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Sources indicate that studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The newly introduced review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

Recent findings suggest that the findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is notable given the average time people take them is much longer.

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

In a recent development, continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

According to recent reports, ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nearly 30 years after 6-year-old JonBenét Ramsey was found dead in her family’s home in Boulder, CO, the tragic case is regaining attention with the release of a new Netflix limited series.

“The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” tells the story of the cold case through a lens that seeks not to solve the mystery, but to tell the story of those who were involved—particularly as the 1996 murder occurred in a decade marked by high-profile crime.

In a recent development, the 1990s "ended with Columbine and started with the Menendez brothers, the Susan Smith murder, the OJ trial,” showrunner Richard LaGravenese stated in a statement. “I was fascinated by the challenge of doing something that was a murder mystery without an ending, without being solved.”.

To portray the effects of the media coverage that surrounded the case, the limited series will focus on Patsy and John Ramsey (played by Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen) as well as a group of local and federal investigators (brought to life by Garrett Hedlund, Will Patton, Shea Whigham, and Alison Pill).

“They all had different points of view for all different reasons,” LaGravenese said. “It was an incredible story to tell from all these perspectives.”.

The Ramsey family’s former home was at the center of the case, and although a handful of interior and exterior shots in the series’ trailer strikingly resemble the recognizable Tudor, it has been reported that “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” was filmed in Calgary, Alberta.

And while a few of the memorable details of the home—such as the black-and-white checkerboard tile floor in the kitchen—also make an appearance in the trailer, much of the home has been updated in recent years. Listing photos from 2024 show that the kitchen was entirely renovated.

Recent findings suggest that the Ramseys purchased the home for $500,000 in 1991, and moved to Atlanta in 1997 following JonBenét’s death. They sold the home for $650,000 in 1998, with profits from the sale pledged to the JonBenét Ramsey Children’s Foundation.

In a recent development, the 7,240-square-foot abode changed hands again, for $1.05 million in 2004. Numerous attempts to sell the home since then have come to naught. In 2008, it was listed for $2.68 million; the price was later reduced to $2.29 million in 2009, $2.3 million in 2011, and $2 million in 2014.

In a recent development, nine years would pass before the home was listed again, asking $6.95 million in March 2023. After a series of price adjustments, the property was taken off the market in February 2025.

In a recent development, jonBenét was found dead in the wine cellar in the basement of the home in the early hours of Dec. 26, 1996. Hours before her body was discovered, the family uncovered a ransom note in the home, which asked $118,000 for the return of their daughter.

Police determined she had been murdered in the late hours of the night on Christmas, and a later autopsy ruled the cause of death as strangulation.

In the following months, police investigated a number of suspects, including Patsy, John, and their son, Burke Ramsey—who were not cleared until July 2008, two years after Patsy died of ovarian cancer.

Dell and HP beat expectations, but their fortunes are diverging as AI dynamics crush the PC market
